about: Proofs of open problems accepted by Lean are merged and credited at once. They count as an open problem solved only once the formal statement has been checked against the original problem (confirmed). flagged: the formal statement does not say what the problem says, so the open problem is not solved. known: listed as open upstream, but already settled in the literature (the Lean proof is a formalization of a known result).

Erdos1066.erdos_1066.variants.higher_dim.note: This is a genuine disproof by construction. It uses a Kerdock-set (Kantor-Williams) two-angle configuration in dimension d=3q (q=2^(2t+1)) with n=2q^2 points. All squared norms are b and all inner products are +-a, with b=1/2+a, so the minimum distance is 1. A Gram-sum argument shows that any subset with all pairwise distances >1 has at most k+2 ~ sqrt(2q)+2 points, whereas c*n/d = 2cq/3; this refutes any uniform constant c. gDim faithfully encodes Erdős's g_d(n). The 'constant independent of d and n' reading is the only meaningful one: erdosproblems.com itself calls the upper bound g_d(n) << n/d 'trivial' via widely spaced simplices, and for fixed d the bound holds with a d-dependent constant (kissing number). erdosproblems.com/1066 is open, with 0 proof claims and no forum comment on the higher-dimensional question. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA110566.conjecture.note: The disproof shows 81 (indeed any multiple of 81) never occurs. v_3(a(n)) = floor(log_3 n) + v_3(H(n)). Using the 3-adic splitting H(n) = H(n/3)/3 + (3-integral part) (cf. Shiu, arXiv:1607.02863), the proof shows v_3(H(n)) + log_3 n <= 3 for all n >= 27, and checks 27 <= n < 81 directly. I independently confirmed numerically that max v_3(a(n)) = 3 for n < 3000 and that 27 occurs but 81 does not. The definition matches OEIS (a(1..6) = 1,1,1,1,1,3), and the conjecture (Jianing Song, 2022) is still listed as open in OEIS. The argument is elementary and close to the classical result J_3 = {2,7,22} (Eswarathasan-Levine), but I found no prior record of the refutation. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA208425.conjecture_2.note: The statement is faithful: a(n) = sum C(n,k)C(n-k,k)C(n+k,k) matches the OEIS formula, and because p = 1 (mod 3) the natural-number divisions 2(p-1)/3 and (p-1)/3 are exact. This is Z.-W. Sun's 2016 conjecture (ii), part 1: sum_{k<p} a(k) = C(2(p-1)/3,(p-1)/3) mod p^2. The proof is a genuine argument. It isolates the exceptional term k=r=(p-1)/3, which yields the binomial coefficient mod p^2, and kills the remaining terms with a finite-field identity, sum over k<=(p-1)/2, k != r, of C(2k,k)/(k-r) = 0 in Z/p. The OEIS entry lists it as a conjecture, and Pan-Sun (Front. Comb. Number Theory 2026, arXiv:2012.05121) prove only part (i). No published proof of (ii) turned up in a search, and the PR cites no prior source. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA260194.conjecture.note: The definition matches OEIS A260194 (three initial 1s, then a(n+3) = a(n+2) + gcd(a(n+2), a(n)), shifted to index 0), and the question 'does every positive integer occur as a difference?' is rendered exactly. The disproof is a genuine finite modular certificate. It proves that from any state whose last two differences are 1, every later difference is at most 89 until the state returns to (1,1); the sequence enters such a state at its start, so the difference 90 never occurs. OEIS still lists this as an open question, and no prior answer turned up. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

RefactorableNumber.zelinsky_refactorable.note: The statement is faithful to Zelinsky (J. Integer Seq. 5 (2002), Art. 02.2.8), Conjecture 32: any arithmetic progression of positive integers that contains a tau (refactorable) number contains infinitely many. The formal version is: for every m>=1 and refactorable n0 there is a larger refactorable n with n = n0 mod m. The proof is a real but very short argument: take a prime p > n0 with p = 1 mod m (Dirichlet) and n = n0*p^{p-1}. Then d(n) = d(n0)*p divides n and n = n0 mod m. Wikipedia still lists the question as unsolved, and nothing in OEIS A033950 records a resolution. Caveat: the argument is elementary enough that it may be folklore. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

Erdos74.erdos_74.variants.sqrt.note: The statement asks for a graph with infinite chromatic number whose n-vertex subgraphs are all within sqrt(n) edge deletions of bipartite. That matches the problem page's 'open even for f(n)=sqrt n'; the max over (not necessarily induced) subgraphs is the same as over induced ones. The main #74 was disproved by GPT-6 Astra only for a very slowly growing f of order log n/log log n, which does not imply the sqrt(n) case. This self-contained disproof proves that any graph with the sqrt(n) local bound has finite chromatic number, via short odd-walk transversals, shell filtrations and ball-carving colourings. erdosproblems shows no sqrt(n) claim. The proof is credited to @preternatural-tocsin (Gemini agent). No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA69004.conjecture2.variants.without_.note: The statement (5a(n) >= pi(n) for all n>1, plus three equalities) is exactly T. D. Noe's lower bound with his claimed equalities; the upper half was already refuted at n=512720. The disproof is a genuine unconditional analytic argument. It takes n = 2^r times many primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), bounds a(n) with Selberg's Lambda^2 sieve, uses the divergence of the product of p/(p-1) over p ≡ 3 (mod 4) via finite Euler products, and uses Chebyshev's lower bound for pi(n). It concludes that 5a(n) < pi(n) for some n. I found no prior refutation of the lower bound in OEIS or upstream. Caveat: this is a minor OEIS empirical remark, and the failure was heuristically expected; the proof is non-constructive. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA179524.conjecture4.note: The statement n | sum_{k<n} (20k+17) a(k) for all n >= 1, with a(n) = sum_k (-4)^k C(n,k)^2 C(n-k,k)^2 (ℕ subtraction is harmless since k <= n), is exactly Z.-W. Sun's 2010 conjecture as recorded in OEIS A179524. The proof is a genuine argument: a telescoping identity reduces the weight, powers of 2 are handled separately, and for the odd part a q-analogue vanishes at odd-order roots of unity, with cyclotomic specialization giving divisibility. OEIS still lists it as a conjecture, and my searches (Sun's open-conjectures list, follow-up papers) found no prior proof. Caveat: Sun's congruence conjectures are heavily studied, so a prior proof in the literature cannot be fully excluded. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA79727.conjecture3.note: The statement a((p^2-1)/2) ≡ p^2 mod p^4 for primes p ≡ 3, 5, 6 mod 7 (OeisA3625.A, with a(n) = sum_{k<=n} C(2k,k)^3) is exactly Peter Bala's Conjecture 3 (July 2024) on OEIS A079727. The proof is a substantial genuine argument: a coefficient of the formal multiplication series of an elliptic curve with CM by Q(sqrt -7), related to a squared Legendre value, plus block cancellation, with p = 3 checked directly. OEIS still lists it as a conjecture (checked up to p = 101), and I found no prior proof. Caveat: the literature search was not exhaustive. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

VCDimConvex.exists_exponential_bound_has.note: HasAddVCNDimAtMost is the standard VC_n-dimension notion for translates: no (d+1)^n sum-grid is shattered. The statement asks for c >= 2 with bound c^n for every convex set in R^{n+1}. The proof gives c = 3 by proving the stronger bounds VC_n <= 2 for n >= 2 and VC_1 <= 3. It is a long, genuine argument: a self-contained Borsuk-Ulam via Ky Fan parity, convex-position cone arguments and chamber surgery. Upstream marks it open, and the only prior result is Kitamura's doubly exponential bound. Caveat: the conjecture is the formal-conjectures authors' own, with no literature source, and the same author's sibling PRs (#2797, #2823) also claim the sharper open variants. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

VCDimConvex.hasAddVCNDimAtMost_n_two_of_.note: The Lean statement is exactly the question asked: for all n>=1, every convex set in R^(n+1) has VC_n dimension at most 3, using the standard HasAddVCNDimAtMost definition, which is non-trivial. The proof is a real 4,300-line argument: a Borsuk-Ulam theorem proved from scratch via Ky Fan parity, Radon for n=1, and chamber surgery for n>=3. As a by-product it proves the sharper bound VC_n <= 2 for n >= 2, which also settles the separately listed open lemma hasAddVCNDimAtMost_two_two_of_convex_r3. The PR does not claim to port earlier work. The only prior results I found are Kitamura's finite bound 2^(8(n+2)^n)-1 and his counterexample to <=1, and I found nothing in the literature on this question. Caveat: the question was posed inside formal-conjectures ('What's not in the literature'), not in a published source, and the argument has no human-written exposition. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

oeis-a262779.note: The formal statement is the conjunction of Colin Barker's two OEIS conjectures for Rule 175 from a single ON cell: a(n) = 101a(n-1) - 100a(n-2) for n > 2, and the g.f. (1+9x+x^2)/((1-x)(1-100x)). Here a(n) is the row of cells -n..n read in base 10, the automaton runs on Z with the rule applied to the background, and the definition reproduces the OEIS data (1, 110, 11011, 1101111, ...). The formalization is faithful; I checked the low-order g.f. coefficients by hand. The proof is genuine. It shows ruleOut 175 = (not l) or r. Induction then shows that for t >= 1 every cell is ON except position 2-t, giving 9a(n) = 10^(2n+1) - 1 - 9*10^(2n-2), from which both claims follow. The entry still lists these as unproved conjectures; OEIS editors in 2022 removed claims that Barker's CA conjectures are proved. I found no earlier proof: A266678 only gives the middle column, and Macfarlane's 2016 paper treats even rule numbers only. Caveat: this is an elementary curve-fit conjecture, not a substantial research problem.

gillibert-equal-halves.note: The formal statement is exactly Gillibert's Equal Halves conjecture (17/11/2026): every finite connected vertex-transitive graph of even order splits as A and its complement, both nonempty, with G[A] and G[Ac] connected and isomorphic. Mathlib's Connected, induce and graph isomorphism are used with no extra hypotheses; the source proves only the Cayley case and leaves the general case open. The disproof exhibits a 28-vertex, 9-regular, non-Cayley vertex-transitive graph (Aut = PSL(2,8), order 504, from the Holt-Royle census). It proves connectivity and vertex-transitivity from explicit automorphisms. An isomorphism of the halves would give a side-swapping involution preserving same-side degree, triangle and distance-2 counts, forcing equal counts of 15 derived predicates on both sides. A kernel-checked bit-plane computation (decide +kernel, no native_decide) shows every balanced 2-colouring violates one of them. This is a real argument, not an encoding exploit. The conjecture is recent and AI-assisted, but it was open at the source, and I found no earlier counterexample. The author's README describes the list as conjectures with nothing known in the literature.

oeis-a263244.note: The formal statement defines the Rule 155 evolution from one ON cell on an OFF background, with every cell updated each step, including the background. It reads cells -n..n as a base-10 digit string. This reproduces the OEIS data (1, 101, 10011, 1011111, ...). It then asserts the conjunction of all conjectured formulas in the entry: Colin Barker's recurrence a(n) = a(n-1) + 10000a(n-2) - 10000a(n-3) for n > 3, his generating function (I checked the coefficients 1, 100, -90, 1100 by hand), and Karl V. Keller's floor formulas for odd and even n. These are exactly the conjectures in the entry, which still labels them as conjectures. The proof is a genuine argument and exploits no loophole: it proves the cell pattern by induction (cell_155_formula), derives closed forms for 9a(n), and from them the step a(n+2) = 10000a(n) + 1111, the recurrence, the power-series identity and the floor formulas. Caveat: this is a routine verification of an empirically fitted formula for a Wolfram class-2 automaton, not a research-level problem. As of this review I found no earlier published proof of these formulas.

mo-236762.note: The MO question (2016, zero answers and no comments as of this review) asks a yes/no question. Let U be a unitary on H = closed span{S_i S_j} in O_infinity that commutes with the flip sigma(S_i S_j) = S_j S_i. Must there be an automorphism of O_infinity that agrees with U on H? The poster suspected NO for U = sigma. The formal statement encodes the YES answer for every C*-algebra generated by a Cuntz family S_i, which by Cuntz uniqueness is O_infinity, with U an inner-product-preserving linear bijection of H commuting with sigma. The disproof proves its negation, so the encoding is faithful. The proof is a genuine argument. If T_i = phi(S_i) were isometries with orthogonal ranges and T_i T_j = S_j S_i, then Q = T_0 T_0^* would satisfy x_N S_0 = S_0 and x_N S_1 = 0, where x_N = S_N^* Q S_N. But on the dense *-algebra spanned by the words S_mu S_nu^*, the compression S_N^* w S_N is eventually a scalar. Approximating Q within 1/3 then gives a contradiction. A concrete model on l^2(N) supplies a nonzero algebra and the flip operator. I found no earlier answer or reference settling this. Caveat: this answers a modest MO question, not a named conjecture, and leaves the poster's follow-up request for a characterisation untouched.

oeis-a346644.note: The formal statement says that every n > 0 is the reduced denominator of sigma(k)/tau(k) for some k > 0, where divisorMean(k) is the rational sum of divisors over number of divisors and Rat.den is the reduced denominator. This is exactly the OEIS conjecture 'k always exists'. The proof is a genuine explicit construction. Write n = 2^v u with u odd, G = 2^(2^v) - 1 and M = uG. Dirichlet's theorem (Mathlib's Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_modEq) gives a prime p = -1 mod 2M. For k = 2^(2^v - 1) p^(M-1), tau(k) = nG and sigma(k) = G(1 + p + ... + p^(M-1)), and the geometric sum is 1 mod 2M, so the reduced denominator is exactly n. I checked the argument and it is correct. The OEIS entry, the related entries A057020 and A057021, and the Bateman-Erdos-Pomerance-Straus paper on the arithmetic mean of divisors contain no proof, and a web search found none. Caveat: the argument is elementary.

oeis-a354478.note: The statement defines rowSum n = Sum_{k=1..n} 1/s(n,k) with signed Stirling numbers of the first kind. This matches Mathematica StirlingS1 and the OEIS data: n=2 gives 0, n=3 gives 7/6. It asserts num/den of rowSum n -> 1, which is exactly Kotesovec's conjecture 'a(n)/A354479(n) tends to 1' (Jun 2022), and the entry still marks it as a conjecture. The proof is a genuine elementary argument. It proves by induction on the Stirling recurrence that n(n-1) <= 2|s(n,k)| for 1 <= k < n and n >= 4, so the n-1 off-diagonal terms contribute at most 2/n while the diagonal term is 1; it exploits no encoding artefact. Neither A354478, A354479 nor a web search turned up an earlier written proof as of this review. Caveat: the result is easy (essentially |s(n,k)| >= C(n,2) off the diagonal), so it is a valid but very minor settlement of an OEIS remark.

oeis-a263245.note: The statement defines Rule 155 from a single ON cell. The rule is applied to the background too, so the background turns ON after step 1, as in the OEIS data. Cells -n..n are read in base 2, and I checked that this reproduces all 1001 b-file terms. It states the conjunction of Colin Barker's conjectured recurrence and g.f. with Karl V. Keller's odd and even closed forms (the ℤ-division exponents are exact under the parity hypotheses), so it faithfully captures the conjectures in the entry. Barker's separate 'Empirical' formula is omitted, but it follows from the g.f. The proof is a genuine induction. It shows that for t ≥ 1 the row is all ON except at position 1-t (odd t), or except at positions 1-t and 2-t (even t). From this it computes a(n) = 3*2^(2n-1) - 1 and 5*2^(2n-2) - 1, then a(n+2) = 16a(n) + 15, and derives the recurrence and g.f. coefficientwise. It uses no native_decide or other tricks. A263245 and its companions A263243/A263244 still label all these formulas as conjectures or empirical, and I found no earlier proof as of this review. The result is mathematically routine (a trivially eventually-periodic automaton), so it is a confirmation of an OEIS-level conjecture, not a significant open problem.

oeis-a379181.note: The source conjecture (Stefano Spezia, Jul 23 2025) is 'a(n+1)/a(n) ~ 10', i.e. the ratio tends to 10; the formal statement is exactly Tendsto (term(n+1)/term(n)) atTop (nhds 10), and the disproof proves its negation. term(n) counts k < 10^n with exactly n digits (0 counted for n=1, so term 1 = 10) whose digit multiset has a unique mode m equal to the mean (sum = m*n), matching the OEIS definition and the Mathematica code Commonest==={Mean}; the n=0 term (0, giving ratio 0 in Lean) does not affect the limit. The proof is a genuine argument: the mean must be an integer, hence at distance >= 1/2 from 4.5, and a digit-flip symmetry plus an exponential-moment (Chernoff-type) bound gives term(n) <= 2*(9.9)^n, whereas a ratio tending to 10 would force term(N+r) >= 9.95^r*term(N), a contradiction via Bernoulli's inequality. The current OEIS entry (rev #27) still lists the conjecture with no refutation, so this disproof is new. The true growth rate is a constrained large-deviation constant strictly below 10, which is consistent with the listed terms (ratios ~9.1-9.6).

oeis-a292727.note: The move relation matches the entry: you pick two equal piles x,x, move 1<=y<=x stones, and drop an emptied pile. a(n) is the number of positive partitions of n not reachable from 1^n. The statement indexes from n>=1 and agrees with the data (a(10)=4 with the listed unreachable states; a(12)=7, a(24)=26, a(20)=9, a(40)=30, a(28)=11, a(56)=34). The two iff conjectures (a(n)=0 iff n is a power of 2, a(n)=1 iff n is an odd prime) are not new: Charlie Neder proved both in the companion entry A292726 (Jan 2019, 'both conjectures are true'), and the proof uses the same odd-divisor invariant. The new part is the pair of formulas a(4p)=p+4 and a(8p)=2p+20, which A292727 still gives only as Neder's conjecture; no proof turned up in a search. The proof derives them from its own lemmas, not by computation for particular p (the only decide calls are partition counts for 4 and 8): reachable_of_pow_two_mul_prime, explicit counts of odd pairs not divisible by p, and ncard_mul_prime. I confirm it on the strength of those two formulas; the iff parts should be credited to Neder.

oeis-a309417.note: A309417 (Moewald, 2019) conjectures that lim a(n+1)/a(n) = 10, where a(n) is the number of steps from 10^n to 0 under x -> x - digitsum(x). term n = countSteps(10^n)(10^n), and the fuel 10^n is enough because each step strictly decreases a positive x. This gives term 1 = 2, matching a(1)=2. Including the extra index n=0 (term 0 = 1) does not change the limit, and term n > 0 is proved, so the real ratio is well defined. The proof is a genuine second-moment argument. The orbit from 10^n visits distinct numbers below 10^n whose digit sums add up to exactly 10^n. Exact second-moment and bounded fourth-moment computations for the digit sum over [0,10^n) show that few numbers have digit sum far from 4.5n. Together these give term n ~ 10^n/(4.5n), so the ratio tends to 10. The entry still lists it as a conjecture with no proof, and a web search found no earlier proof.

oeis-a108629.note: The statement encodes the g.f. (1+x-sqrt(1-2x-3x^2-4x^3))/(2+2x+2x^2) over Q, taking the square-root branch with constant term 1 via binomialSeries(1/2) composed with -2X-3X^2-4X^3. With a(n) = coeff n, a(0)=0 and a(1)=1, which matches OEIS offset 1 (1,0,1,2,4,11,...). The recurrence is exactly R. J. Mathar's 'Conjecture D-finite with recurrence' (Jan 2020), stated for n>=6 where every index is defined; I checked it by hand at n=6 (66=66). The proof is a genuine algebraic derivation. It uses R^2 = 1+t to get 2(1+t)R' = t'R, substitutes R = 1+X-2(1+X+X^2)A to get a first-order linear ODE for A, and reads off coefficients. The entry still marks the recurrence as conjectural. The result is routine (any algebraic g.f. is D-finite), so its novelty is low, but no earlier proof exists in the source.

mo-348551.note: The question (no answers; only David Handelman's comment that it is unlikely to be tractable) asks to show that phi_i(k) = (lambda_i - lambda_{i+1})/k is unimodal, where lambda_j are the ordered eigenvalues of (A^T)^k A^k / rho(A)^{2k} and A is any entrywise nonnegative matrix. The formalisation is faithful: it requires positive Perron root (needed for the division, and noted in the comments), lists eigenvalues with multiplicity in decreasing order, uses k>0, and defines unimodality as nondecreasing up to k0 and nonincreasing after, which matches the source's definition. The disproof uses A = [1] (+) [[0,1],[1/4,0]] with rho=1. At even times the normalized Gram matrix is diag(1,16^-m,16^-m); at odd times it is diag(1,16^-m/16,16^-m) up to order. So phi_2 alternates between 0 and a positive value and cannot be unimodal for any k0, under the MO definition as well. The 2x2 irreducible block alone already gives a counterexample, so nonnegative matrices are definitely not unimodal in general. The argument is genuine and elementary. The only caveat is that the asker might have meant primitive matrices, but did not say so.

oeis-a229623.note: The OEIS entry gives the data 0,1,...,9,11,101,...,929,1001,10001,... with offset 1, and Derek Orr's 2015 conjecture a(n) = 10^(n-18)+1 for n>20. The statement uses Nat.nth qualifies (n-1) with qualifies m := digits(m) palindrome and digits(m - digitsum m) palindrome, which matches: nth 0 = 0 and the 21st term is 1001 = 10^3+1. Range n>=21 is correct and there is no weakening. The proof is a real digit argument. For an L-digit palindrome m >= 10^4 the digit sum s < 10^(L/2). If m-s loses a digit, then m = 10^(L-1)+1. If the top half is unchanged, mirroring forces 10^(L/2) | s, which is impossible. Otherwise a borrow forces s = 10^q mod 10^(q+1) with s <= 18(q+1), also impossible. The finite range below 10^4 is checked with decide. Neither the entry nor A229621 marks the conjecture as proved, and I found no earlier proof.

arxiv-2404.06445.note: Conjecture 8.9 ('Main Conjecture') of Mallik, Diwan and Kothari v3 says that every minimal k-extendable bipartite graph has |V_{k+1}| ≥ 2/(2k-1)·(m - n + 2k). The formal statement matches the paper's Section 8 definitions: connected, order ≥ 2k+2, has a k-matching, every k-matching extends to a perfect matching, minimal under edge deletion, V_{k+1} = vertices of degree exactly k+1, no extra order threshold. The disproof is an explicit 16-vertex bipartite graph with k = 3. H_A–L_B and L_A–H_B are complete (|H| = 3, |L| = 5), plus a perfect matching between L_A and L_B and one edge between H_A and H_B, for m = 36 and only 10 vertices of degree 4, below the bound 52/5 = 10.4. I checked this independently by brute force: the graph is connected and bipartite, every 3-matching extends to a perfect matching, every single-edge deletion destroys 3-extendability, and it is consistent with Lou's theorem and with the paper's Conjecture 8.10 (tight at 10). It does not use small-order degeneracy, since n = 16 ≥ 8. I found no earlier counterexample: the only later paper on these bounds (He, arXiv 2611.29504, confirming Conjecture 8.11 for k ≥ 3) does not address 8.9.

oeis-a122251.note: The formal statement matches Paul Barry's 2006 general conjecture. For every prime p and every n, the reduced numerator of det[1/(1+p(i+j))] over 0≤i,j≤n equals (p^2)^{sum_{k=1..n} sum_{j=0..n} floor(k/p^j)}. I checked n=1, p=3: det = 9/112. The companion entry A122249 (p=2) still says 'Conjecture - requires proof', and I found no proof in the OEIS or in the literature I searched; arXiv 2607.18644 handles different Barry conjectures. The proof is a genuine argument. It eliminates the last pivot to get det_{t+1} = det_t·(p^t t!/prod_i(1+p(i+t)))^2/(1+2pt). It then uses a classical divisibility fact: the part of t! coprime to p divides the product of t consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression with step p. So the denominator is coprime to p and the numerator is exactly p^{2(t+v_p(t!))} at each step, which sums to the conjectured exponent. The argument is elementary, but I found no earlier source for it.

oeis-a401159.note: T(n,m) is formalised as the number of labelled Bool-matrices on Fin n x Fin m with at most two trues per row and per column. The two conjectures (Mathar, Nov 18 2026) appear as T(n,2) = A086601(n) = (1+n+C(n,2))^2 and 8T(n,3) = 8+8n+22n^2+13n^3+n^4+3n^5+n^6. These match the entry: A086601 = A000124^2, the denominator 8 is cleared, and the restriction to n≥m is the triangle's own domain. The T(n,2) half is close to trivial, because a row of length 2 can never break its limit, so the two columns are independent subsets of size at most 2. The proof says exactly this. For T(n,3) the proof uses inclusion-exclusion over the triples of column-sets whose common intersection is nonempty, and derives T + n·n^3 = (1+n+C(n,2))^3 + C(n,2). Mathar's 2014 paper only tabulates the values and gives no closed forms. The entry is new and labels both formulas as conjectures, so this is a correct and faithful proof of two easy but recent conjectures; I found no earlier source.

oeis-a057663.note: The statement is faithful to Gerasimov's 2019 conjecture: for k≥1, φ(k+2^k) = φ(k)+2^k holds exactly when k and k+2^k are both prime. The k≥1 restriction matches a sequence of positive integers. I found no other OEIS entry that mentions the identity, and A057663 still calls it a conjecture. The proof is genuine and elementary. Suppose N = k+2^k is composite with least prime factor p. Then N - φ(N) ≥ N/p ≥ sqrt(N) ≥ k, using k^2 ≤ k+2^k. That contradicts N - φ(N) = k - φ(k) < k. Hence N is prime, so φ(k) = k-1, which forces k to be prime. The conjecture is easy, but no earlier proof was found.

mo-309804.note: The formal statement is faithful. A is real upper triangular with negative diagonal, so it is Hurwitz with real spectrum. X and P are symmetric positive definite (Mathlib PosDef includes symmetry), tr X = 1, AP+PA^T = -X, and the objective is tr(X(I+P)^{-1}). The set of values is nonempty and bounded by 1, so Lean's sSup convention cannot trivialise the claim, and the target 2trA/(2trA-1) lies in (0,1). On MathOverflow the question has only two partial answers (an orthogonal-invariance remark and first-order conditions) and comments, none of which settles it. The proof is a genuine argument. Using tr(XP^{-1}) = -2trA, a Kakutani fixed-point step (Brouwer/Kakutani code adapted from harfe's MIT repository, with attribution) gives a PSD trace-one state supported on a single eigenspace of P, whose eigenvalue c must equal -1/(2trA). That state attains 1/(1+c) = 2trA/(2trA-1), and a regularisation step approaches it from the positive definite side. The proof also gives the reverse inequality through a tangent bound, so it establishes the asker's numerically observed equality. I found no earlier solution.

oeis-a033955.note: The statement is faithful to Alonso del Arte's conjecture (Jul 27 2026): for n>6 (1-based), the sum of prime(n) mod prime(k) over k<n exceeds prime(n). With the zero-based Nat.nth, 5<n is exactly the 1-based n>6, and the sum runs over the n smaller primes. The bound is strict and the threshold is correct, since a(6)=13=prime(6). The conjecture is recent and the entry gives no proof. The proof is genuine. For p ≥ 65536 it uses Mathlib's Chebyshev theta bounds to show that the primes in (p/3, p) contribute enough remainder. It then checks 256 ≤ p < 65536 with kernel-verified block certificates and 17 ≤ p < 256 with explicit rows.

oeis-a283508.note: The formal model follows the entry's Mathematica program. The rule bit is selected at index centre + 2·(von Neumann neighbour count) in 643, all cells of the infinite grid update, the origin is read first through (n,0) as decimal digits, and Rule 187 is used for A267623. The statement packages all four empirical conjectures: Barker's generating function, closed form and recurrence, and Mathar's a(n) = A267623(n). The proof is a genuine, if easy, argument. Rule 643 turns on cells that have no ON neighbours, so after two steps the grid reaches a fixed pattern in which every cell is ON except the 8 around the origin. Rule 187 sends the single ON cell to a moving 'hole' row. Both give the digit string 1,0,1,1,1,..., and the three formulas follow. The entry still labels these as conjectures and I found no earlier written proof, so I confirm it, while noting that the content is a routine calculation.

OeisA113258.conjecture.note: The DeepMind statement defines a n = sum_{i<n} (i+1)!^((n-i)!), which equals the OEIS formula sum_{i=1..n} (i!)^((n-i+1)!). It asks for some n > 4, b > 1, e > 1 with a n = b^e, which is exactly Vos Post's question 'Is there a nontrivial power after a(4) = 5^3?'. The disproof shows no later term is a perfect power. This is a substantial argument of about 7400 lines with no sorry and no custom axiom (CI audits axioms). It shows: (1) 2^((n-1)!) < a(n) < 2^((n-1)!) + 2^(4(n-2)!), so any exponent prime p must satisfy p >= n; (2) explicit prime-modulus witnesses rule out n = 5..8 and every (n,p) in the remaining finite range; (3) a formalised special case of Laurent's lower bound for linear forms in two logarithms (interpolation-determinant proof, `LaurentTwoLog`, `direct_log_bound`) bounds p for large n. I found no earlier resolution. The OEIS entry still asks the question, and all four Epoch OEIS-Open runs on this problem (OpenAI, GDM, Anthropic, Gemini) scored I (incorrect). This looks like a genuine new result, not a weakening.

oeis-a214074.note: The statement faithfully encodes Kimberling's 2012 conjecture: for n >= 1, the least m > 0 with gcd(2^n - m, 3^n - m) = 1 is 3 if and only if n = 330k - 209 for some k >= 1. The integer gcd handles negative values correctly. The disproof takes n = 3438721 = 330*10421 - 209. Modulo the prime 487891, both 2^n and 3^n are 3; I re-checked this independently, and 487891 has no divisor below its square root. So 487891 divides gcd(2^n - 3, 3^n - 3), 3 is not in the set, and the 'if' direction fails; the exponent progression 3438721 + 5366790t gives infinitely many counterexamples. This is a genuine, non-trivial counterexample: the exhibited counterexample n ≈ 3.4 million lies far beyond the 1000-term b-file, and finding it needs a search for a prime obstruction of this size. The OEIS entry and the related entries (A214180, A214707-A214709) still list the conjecture unrefuted. Neither the Epoch OEIS-Open paper nor Fried's 2026 OEIS-conjecture paper mentions A214074. I found no earlier refutation.

OeisA79727.conjecture2.note: The statement is that a(p(p-1)) = p^2 mod p^3 for primes p = 3, 5, 6 mod 7 (OeisA3625.A), with a(n) = sum_{k<=n} C(2k,k)^3. This is exactly Peter Bala's Conjecture 2 (July 2024) on OEIS A079727, which still lists it as a conjecture. I checked numerically that it holds for p = 3, 5, 13, 17, 19. The proof (about 3960 lines, no sorry or native_decide, with p=3 done separately) is a substantial original argument. It expands a(p(p-1)) mod p^3 in blocks and uses the supersingular CM curve y^2 = (x+21)(x^2+7) (Hasse invariant), a 2-isogeny and Picard-Fuchs/Wronskian identities. It is in the same family as the already-confirmed OeisA79727.conjecture3. Searches found only Zhi-Hong Sun's mod p^2 result for a(p-1) and unrelated mod p^3 supercongruences (e.g. arXiv:2408.09776, arXiv:2610.34160), no proof of this congruence. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

OeisA157237.conjecture.note: The definition matches OEIS: a(n) counts (x,y), x,y>=1, with 2n-1-2^x-11*2^y prime and ≡ 1 (mod 6). The Lean 'iff' statement is Sun's conjecture exactly. The disproof is an explicit counterexample n=333811606269876, i.e. 2n-1 = 667623212539751, with every candidate difference shown ≡/≡ 1 mod 6 or given an explicit proper divisor. I independently checked that all 549 differences ≡ 1 (mod 6) are composite, so a(n)=0, and n is not one of the listed exceptions. OEIS records only verification below 1.5*10^8 and no counterexample, and searches found no earlier record of this number or a refutation. No earlier proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

Erdos473.erdos_473.variants.finite.note: The statement (for every n >= 2 there is a permutation of {1..n}, via Fin n ≃ Fin n shifted by 1, with all adjacent sums prime) is exactly Segal's finite question on erdosproblems.com/473. The page says it is open and 'true for infinitely many n' via bounded prime gaps; van Doorn in the forum knew no proof. The closest prior work is Y.-F. She (arXiv:2609.19114, 16 Sep 2026), who proves that prime circles of order 2n exist for all sufficiently large n. That would give the path version for all large n, but with an ineffective n0, so the all-n statement was not established. OEIS A051252 still says there is no proof for all n. The 10.6k-line proof is fully effective: strong induction with reflection primes, explicit prime counts in (33N/34, N] for N >= 9.1*10^19 via a certified sieve, and certified small cases. No sorry or axioms. No earlier complete proof was found as of this review; corrections welcome.

mo-136792.note: The statement matches the question: standard Borel spaces as Polish spaces, K analytic, g Borel, h measurable for sigma(analytic sets), (x,y) in K with g(x,y)=h(x) for every x; is there an analytically measurable lift f? The disproof builds a counterexample by a diagonal argument over well-founded Borel codes for sigma(Sigma^1_1) sets. The MO question (2013) has 0 answers; George Lowther only guessed 'no' in a comment. I found no published counterexample, but this could be folklore descriptive set theory, so an expert check is advisable.

mo-200855.note: The formal statement is the asker's conjecture word for word: symmetric 0/1 adjacency with zero diagonal, g12=g13=1, g23=0, 0<lambda<1/(n-1), y1>=y2 and y1>=y3 imply x1/y1 > y3/z3, where x and z are the Katz-type scores after deleting 12 and adding 23. The question (2015) has no answers, and the asker checked n<=8 only. The disproof gives an explicit 15-vertex graph at t=1/30, with the scores computed exactly from integer solutions. The disproof is a finite counterexample check.

mo-352184.note: The formal statement ('every score-class contains a fair-indexed tournament') is the natural reading of the 2020 question, which has 0 answers. The comment-thread counterexamples (22225555 and others) concern stronger variants or monotone orderings, not the question itself. The disproof is an exhaustive kernel search: for n=16, no fair-indexed tournament has scores 3^4 9^12, and a tournament with those scores exists. This genuinely answers the question (no), and it is a finite check.

oeis-a028886.note: Kurkov's criterion (Dec 2025): (2m+1)^2-8 is prime iff q(m+1)+C(q,2)+1 is never a square for 1<=q<=2(m-2); the formal statement is exact. Setting X=2q+2m+1 turns the square condition into N=X^2-8s^2, so the claim is that N is composite iff it has a second representation by x^2-8y^2 in a range. The proof does genuine arithmetic in Z[sqrt2] (Euclidean division, norms, factor splitting). No earlier proof found; the entry still lists it as a conjecture.

oeis-a047872.note: McEachen's 2021 conjecture: a(n)=floor(|B(2n+2)/B(2n)|) = floor((n+1)(2n+1)/(2 pi^2)). The statement is faithful. The ratio equals x_n*zeta(2n+2)/zeta(2n) with x_n=(n+1)(2n+1)/(2pi^2), so the claim needs frac(x_n) to exceed about n^2 4^{-n}. The proof checks n<2048 by interval bounds and handles large n with an explicit Beukers-integral irrationality-measure bound for pi^2 (Hanson lcm bound). That is a substantive argument. The entry still says 'conjectured', and I found no earlier proof.

oeis-a071284.note: Barker's period-10 conjecture for the denominators of the order-4 Peirce sequence. I simulated the formal insertion model, and it reproduces the entry's example rows for orders 1-5 (e.g. order 4: 2,4,3,1,4,3,4,2,...), so the encoding is faithful. Periodicity follows from the translation-invariant insertion rule. Routine.

oeis-a102827.note: Van der Sanden's conjecture: in every base the 'True already' sequence has no term divisible by the base. The formal definition follows the entry: least positive x whose last digit d has been written exactly floor(x/b) times so far, with no monotonicity required. I simulated it independently: it matches the data and Mathar's a(99)=212, and gives a(332)=20 right after a(331)=1002 creates the first two zeros. Genuine counterexample in base 10, finite check; no earlier report found.

oeis-a132304.note: Bala's Aug 2025 conjecture: a(np^k) == a(np^{k-1}) (mod p^{2k}) for primes p>=5 and n,k>=1, where a(n) = sum_k T(n,k)^4 over trinomial coefficients. The statement is exact. The 690-line proof is a genuine supercongruence argument: it clears denominators in binomial and multiset-binomial products, pairs i with pj-i, uses (1+x+x^2)=(1-x^3)/(1-x), and the fourth power kills off-grid terms. The entry still lists it as a conjecture; the nearest literature (Otmani-Belbachir 2025, central trinomial supercongruences) does not cover it. The proof notes that the cube case A132303 was done earlier by @rbajaj5 on GitHub.

oeis-a151341.note: Mathar's 2017 recurrence for a(n) = Catalan(n)*Motzkin(n). The statement defines a by that product, which the entry lists as a (non-conjectural) formula, and proves the three-term P-recursive identity. Routine holonomic identity.

oeis-a158233.note: Curtz's 2009 conjecture that the terms lie in {0,3,4,6}. The triangle reading and offsets match the entry's controls (I recomputed 20000 terms: values {0,3,4,6}). The proof is a residue-class analysis of (m^2-n^2) products mod 9. Routine.

oeis-a165640.note: Layman's floor formula for the multisets of -2, 1, 3 with n members and sum 3. The statement counts the multiplicity triples exactly. Solving the two linear equations reduces this to a lattice-point count, so the formula is routine.

oeis-a178297.note: Mathar's 2010 closed form 2a(n) = 11^n + 5*9^n - 6*7^n for collinear 6-subsets of {0..6}^n. The statement counts 6-sets whose real images are collinear. The formula follows from classifying grid lines with 6 or 7 points by coordinate patterns (constant, increasing or decreasing) and checks against the data. A routine but careful count (836-line proof); no earlier proof found.

oeis-a182025.note: Mathar's 2012 recurrence for 31C(2n,n-4) + sum C(2n,n-4-i)(4+i). The statement handles n<4 explicitly, as in the data. A routine holonomic (Zeilberger-type) identity.

oeis-a191625.note: Mathar's 2017 order-9 recurrence for two-sided prudent walks ending at the NE corner. The formal walk definition (prudent ray condition, top-or-right prefixes, final corner) matches Bousquet-Melou's. The entry gives Bousquet-Melou's proven algebraic g.f., and the recurrence follows from it mechanically. The 2100-line proof re-derives the kernel equation. Routine consequence of a known g.f.

oeis-a192473.note: Barker's recurrence for the x-coefficient of 1+x^n+x^{2n+2} mod x^2-x-1. Since x^k reduces to F_k x + F_{k-1}, this is a Fibonacci identity. Routine.

oeis-a192940.note: Mathar's recurrence for the x-coefficient of (x+2)(x+4)...(x+2n) mod x^2-x-1. It follows by multiplying the reduced pair by (x+2n) at each step. Routine.

oeis-a195915.note: Adams-Watters's observation T(2^j+n, 2^j+k) = T(n,k) for 2^j>n. The 0-based column indices and the bound k<n translate the 1-based source correctly. A 30-line XOR/Pascal-mod-2 induction. Routine.

oeis-a203232.note: Mathar's recurrence a(n)=12a(n-2)-36a(n-4) and g.f. for the (n-1)-st elementary symmetric function of (2,3,2,3,...). Routine.

oeis-a216211.note: Barker's 2017 rational g.f. (and order-12 recurrence) for self-avoiding walks from NW to SW corner in an n x 4 grid. The walk definition matches the data, including count(1)=1. The proof is a finite transfer-matrix computation. Routine.

oeis-a223906.note: Barker's closed form a(n)=2^{n+1}+3^{n+1}+4^n and g.f. With |s(3,1)|,|s(3,2)|,|s(3,3)| = 2,3,1 it is immediate from the defining sum. Routine.

oeis-a233398.note: Dale's 2025 conjecture n^n mod 3^n = 0 when 3|n. Trivial: (3y)^{3y} = 3^{3y} y^{3y}. A 3-line proof.

oeis-a248521.note: Kotesovec's 2014 conjecture a(n) ~ pi n/2. The formal statement is the source condition (Nat.nth enumerator, ratio -> pi/2). Since cot(pi/(2k)) = 2k/pi + O(1/k) has increments below 1, the number of selected k <= K is the floor at K+1, about 2K/pi. Routine asymptotics.

oeis-a257838.note: Mathar's 2015 recurrence for the diagonal of iterated Fibonacci partial sums. The indexing is shifted correctly. Routine holonomic identity.

oeis-a262009.note: Hanna's 2015 conjectures on the 2-adic valuation of sum_{d|n} 2^{d^2}(n/d)^2. The d=1 term has valuation 2v_2(n)+1, strictly smaller than every other term, which gives both claims at once. Routine.

oeis-a266249.note: Barker's closed form, recurrence and g.f. for the ON cells of Rule 9. The conventions follow the entry's Mathematica program (background updated, cells -n..n) and reproduce the data. An eventually periodic pattern proved by induction. Routine.

oeis-a266607.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. for the Rule 39 row values. The conventions follow the entry's program and reproduce the controls. Routine pattern induction.

oeis-a267262.note: Barker's closed form, recurrence and g.f. for the cumulative OFF cells of Rule 111. The conventions follow the program, and the controls match. Routine.

oeis-a267774.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. for the Rule 207 row values. The conventions follow the program, and the controls match. Routine.

oeis-a273446.note: Blomberg's 2016 conjectures: Rule 729 gives the same counts as Rule 721 at stages 2^n-1, and a(n)=4*4^n-4*2^n for n>2. The outer-totalistic convention and the central-square count follow the program (controls 1,4,41). A routine pattern induction for a 2D CA.

oeis-a283648.note: Barker's g.f., parity closed forms and recurrence for the Rule 705 x-axis. The conventions follow the program, and the controls match. Routine.

oeis-a294513.note: Lang's 2017 conjecture a(n) = 2*A250327(n+1)/(n+1). The statement is faithful (computed in Q, A250327 as the numerator of the harmonic mean of pentagonal numbers). I recomputed it independently: it holds for n<1891 and fails at n=1891 (1892 = 4*11*43, and the RHS is not an integer: a leftover factor 1/11). A genuine counterexample by finite computation; not noted in the entry.

oeis-a303647.note: Barker's 2018 recurrence and g.f., plus the corrected (Sep 2026) A301483/A195350/A195339 identity, for a(n) = ceil(a(n-1)/(2^{1/3}-1)+1). r=1/(2^{1/3}-1) is a cubic Pisot number (r^3-3r^2-3r-1=0). The proof uses the standard model-sequence and error-bound argument. Routine Pisot-type argument.

oeis-a325695.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. for strict 3-part partitions whose largest part is not the sum of the other two. A quasi-polynomial lattice-point count. Routine.

oeis-a329227.note: Barker's g.f. for products of consecutive Padovan numbers. Routine linear-recurrence identity.

oeis-a333686.note: Manyama's conjectured g.f. and recurrence for self-avoiding paths in a (2n+1) x 3 grid through the centre. The walk definition matches the data. The 3400-line proof is a 5-state transfer-matrix argument. Routine in method.

oeis-a337951.note: Hanna's mod-5 congruences for 4^{n(n-1)/2}+4^{n(n+1)/2}. Immediate from 4 == -1 (mod 5) and the parity of triangular numbers. Routine.

oeis-a370261.note: Bala's 2024 integrality conjecture for sqrt(A370259(2n)/(n+1)). From T_{2n}(x)-1 = 2(x^2-1)U_{n-1}(x)^2 with x=2n+1, the quantity is (U_{n-1}(2n+1)/n)^2, and n | U_{n-1}(2n+1) because U_{n-1}(1)=n. Routine Chebyshev identity.

oeis-a374192.note: Detlefs's 2024 conjecture that the modified Collatz map reaches 1 or 10. The step function matches. The proof is a 40-line strong induction: two to four steps always give a smaller value. Routine.

oeis-a382437.note: The binomial-sum formula for a(n)=a(n-1)^2+4a(n-1), a(0)=2. Here a(n)+2 = 2T_{2^n}(2), and the sum is the standard expansion of 2T_m(1+y/2)-2 at y=2. Routine.

oeis-a383702.note: Mathar's 2025 recurrence for the x^2 coefficient of prod (x+4j+3). Routine holonomic identity.

mo-202165.note: The statement encodes Propp's relation faithfully on Z. Pieces are binned by the left endpoint of a window of width r, which is harmless since each site has finite mass. Equal mass and equal first moment is the same as equal mass and equal centre of mass. The proof establishes transitivity (with width 12(max r t + 1)) by a non-trivial prefix/blend construction. On MO, Propp thought the relation was not transitive and C. Remling's attempted proof was withdrawn as imprecise. No earlier solution was found.

mo-363072.note: The statement matches the revised MO question: A has zero line sums, is >=0 on the graph of sigma and <=0 off it, B is doubly stochastic and sigma maximises B's assignment sum, conclusion <A,B>_F >= 0. The proof is a short but non-obvious Birkhoff-von Neumann trick: S = P_sigma - A/m is doubly stochastic for m = 1 + sum A_{i,sigma(i)}, so <A,B> = m(<P_sigma,B> - <S,B>) >= 0. The question had no answers in six years. A correct, new, short argument.

mo-138395.note: The statement is the classical inequality alpha H(X) + (1-alpha) H(Y) >= K^2 H(Z) for all n and alpha in [0,1]. It adds the hypothesis K>0, which the question needs for Z to be a probability measure, and uses rpow conventions that only matter at alpha in {0,1}. Only alpha=1/2 (fedja, MO 138275) was proved before. The two answers to 138395 are not proofs. The 65 KB proof (reduction to three atoms, then a binary log-odds convexity argument) is substantive. The quantum, non-commuting extension asked at the end of the question is not covered.

mse-199784.note: The statement matches the question: m,n>1, all entries +-1, no non-trivial row/column permutation pair fixes A, and a unique Nash equilibrium that is fully mixed. Excluding the 1x1 case only strengthens the claim. The proof gives an explicit symmetric 7x7 +-1 matrix with equilibrium weights (i+1)/28. A is invertible, which gives uniqueness, and the distinct weights force total asymmetry. The 2012 question had no answers (a comment ruled out 4xn and 5x5). An explicit witness checked by finite computation; the open part was finding it.

oeis-a002742.note: The statement faithfully encodes the e.g.f. (2x/(1-x^2) + log(1-x^2)) e^{-x} and both of Bala's congruences (2k | a(n+2k) - a(n), (2k+1) | a(n+2k+1) + a(n)). The proof rewrites a(n) as a signed binomial transform of explicit factorial weights and uses standard binomial-sum divisibility. No prior proof found; elementary and short.

oeis-a026008.note: Mathar's five-term P-recurrence for an explicit binomial closed form (Ralf Stephan's formulas, checked against the data). The shift n=t+4 is correct. A routine holonomic-recurrence verification.

oeis-a038663.note: Kotesovec's a(n) ~ (A079586 - 1) n. The constant is encoded correctly: sum over F_1, F_2, ... minus 1 matches floors over F_2, F_3, .... Immediate, since the floor error is O(log n). Routine.

oeis-a048330.note: Mathar's g.f. and the recurrence a(n) = 6a(n-4) - 5a(n-8) for base-5 repdigits (0 included, as in the data). A direct consequence of the explicit form d*(5^k-1)/4. Routine.

oeis-a051195.note: Mathar's P-recurrence for the count of aperiodic binary words of length 2n+2 with n ones. The definition matches the data. By Moebius inversion a(n) = C(2n+2,n) - [n even] C(n+1,n/2), so the recurrence is a holonomic identity. Routine.

oeis-a057300.note: Ralf Stephan's two recurrences for the base-4 digit swap 1<->2. The definition matches the data. A direct digit-level induction. Routine.

oeis-a062071.note: Kotesovec's a(n) ~ c n with c = sum 1/k^k. Immediate: floor errors are bounded by the number of k with k^k <= n. Routine.

oeis-a088276.note: This disproves both parts of the conjecture with r = 162207 (odd, not divisible by 5, == 0 mod 3). 10^k + 162207 is always divisible by one of 11, 101, 73, 137 (covering mod 8), so the entry is 0 and there are no primes at all. The formal statement is faithful. The covering is the dual of Pierre Cami's covering for 162207*10^k+1 in A244348, so the counterexample is a finite check built on existing data. Not previously noted against A088276.

oeis-a092765.note: The statement matches Bala's stronger congruence a(np^k) == a(np^(k-1)) mod p^(2k) for p != 3. a(n) is the constant term of (x^-2+x^-1+x+x^2)^n, encoded as [x^{2n}](1+x+x^3+x^4)^n and checked against the data. The proof uses a(n) = sum_j C(n,j) C(n,2n-3j) and a termwise Jacobsthal-style pairing argument. No earlier proof found. A genuine supercongruence, though by standard techniques.

oeis-a112032.note: Barker's recurrence a(n) = 2a(n-2) and g.f. (x+4)/(1-2x^2) for the denominators of the partial sums. The terms are encoded correctly. Immediate from the closed form of the partial sums. Routine.

oeis-a113768.note: Grau Ribas's a(n) ~ (2/3) n sqrt((2/3) n) for a(n+1) = a(n) + floor(a(n)^(1/3)). The index shift is harmless. A standard difference-equation asymptotic (a^{2/3} grows like 2n/3). Routine.

oeis-a127711.note: Barry's integrality conjecture is trivial. The triangle is diag(1/F(n+1)) times a 0/1 lower unitriangular matrix, so its inverse is an integer unitriangular inverse times diag(F(n+1)). The formal statement (all finite leading blocks) is faithful. Routine.

oeis-a132305.note: The statement matches Bala's 2025 supercongruence for sums of fifth powers of trinomial coefficients, a(np^k) == a(np^(k-1)) mod p^(2k), p>=5. The proof uses clearing denominators, pairing i with pj-i, and (1+x+x^2) = (1-x^3)/(1-x). A related cube case existed in a GitHub note (rbajaj5); no prior proof of the fifth-power case was found. A genuine supercongruence proof.

oeis-a136433.note: Mathar's recurrence a(n) = 6a(n-3) + a(n-6) - 6a(n-9) for a linear recurrence with period-6 coefficients. The definition matches the data. A finite case split on n mod 6. Routine.

oeis-a152661.note: Both Mathar conjectures (the P-recurrence and a(n) = 2*A077613(n-1)) for the closed form (e(e-1)+o(o-1))(n-2)!. The closed forms match both sequences' data. Routine.

oeis-a167481.note: Mathar's P-recurrence for the convolution sum (-2)^{n-k} C(2k,k). A routine holonomic verification.

oeis-a175764.note: f(k) is the smallest prime factor of k^2+4. Conjecture 1 is immediate: even n gives 2, n == +-1 mod 10 gives 5, and n>29 is not a target. Conjecture 2: those classes mod 130 have spf(n^2+4) = 13, since no prime below 13 can divide n^2+4, and 13 reaches 5 in 8 more steps. The formal IsLeast encoding is faithful. The entry itself asked 'are these conjectures easy to prove?' Yes, routine.

oeis-a178298.note: Mathar's closed form 7^n - 5^(n+1)/2 + 13^n/2 + 9^n for collinear 3-subsets of {0..4}^n. Real collinearity is used, and the definition reproduces 0, 10, 152, 1858. A finite-pattern counting argument (coordinatewise classification of collinear triples). Elementary combinatorics.

oeis-a183003.note: Irvine's conjecture: A183003 is the partial sums of A072670. Since ij+i+j = m iff (i+1)(j+1) = m+1, it is a direct divisor-pair count. Routine.

oeis-a192480.note: Mathar's P-recurrence for n + Catalan(n-1). It is stated for n>=4 because it fails at n=2,3 (checked numerically: -2 and -6) owing to the exceptional initial terms; this is the usual reading of Mathar's recurrences. A routine holonomic verification.

oeis-a192941.note: Mathar's recurrence for the constant term of (2x+1)...(2x+n) mod x^2-x-1. The definition matches the entry's examples. Routine.

oeis-a197918.note: p XOR q = p - q iff q's bits are a subset of p's. So a term other than 2, 5, 17 cannot have bit 1 (q=2), bit 2 (q=5) or bit 4 (q=17) set, which is exactly p XOR 22 = p + 22. Trivial.

oeis-a217280.note: Lucas's theorem plus Fermat (2^{5^i} == 2 mod 5) give a(n) == prod a(digit) mod 5. With a(0..4) == 1, 0, 1, 0, 0 mod 5 this is exactly the digit-{0,2} rule. Routine.

oeis-a226224.note: For b>=3, k=(b-1)^2 has base-b digits (1, b-2) summing to b-1. For b=2, popcount(r^2) < r for r>=2, with a finite check for small r. Trivial.

oeis-a233578.note: Kaarhus's criterion follows from von Staudt-Clausen. With m = den/6, num(B_n) == m (mod 6), and the sign of B_n (n mod 4) with 5 | m iff 4 | n gives exactly the residues {1,5,7,13,19} mod 30. Odd n are handled (B_n = 0). Routine.

oeis-a247339.note: Let p = spf(n^2+1) and m the least positive root of m^2 == -1 mod p. Then m <= n and m < p/2, so m^2+1 = p*c with c < p, hence gpf(m^2+1) = p (and p=2 gives m=1). This is the classical argument. The formalization is faithful. Routine.

oeis-a259714.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. for a convolution recurrence with periodic weights (k mod 5). The definition matches the data. A rational g.f. identity. Routine.

oeis-a266251.note: Barker's closed form, recurrence and g.f. for the OFF cells of Rule 9, with the background evolving as in the entry's program and the data controls matching. The pattern becomes periodic, so this is a finite-structure induction. Routine.

oeis-a266790.note: Barker's closed form and g.f. for the middle column of Rule 61 read in base 10, with the data controls matching. The column becomes eventually periodic. Routine.

oeis-a267461.note: Barker's closed form, recurrence and g.f. for the cumulative OFF cells of Rule 133, with the controls matching. Eventually periodic rows. Routine.

oeis-a267920.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. for Rule 243 rows read in base 10. The background turning ON at t=1 matches the data (101, 11101, ...). Routine.

oeis-a275667.note: Zabolotskii's recurrences for the triangular odd-rule CA. The F2 group-algebra model (stencil with alternating orientation) reproduces all 59 OEIS terms (checked in Python). The proof uses the standard odd-rule/Frobenius technique (cf. the Ekhad-Sloane-Zeilberger meta-algorithm linked in the entry). Saadat-Nagy proved only pattern replication. No prior proof of these recurrences found.

oeis-a294515.note: This genuinely disproves Lang's conjecture a(n) = A250550(n+1)/(n+1), which is equivalent to gcd(n+1, num V(n)) = 1. The counterexample is n = 491244 = 19*25855 - 1, where 19 divides the numerator of V(n), established by a 19-adic block argument. My Python check found no failure for n < 400. The formal definitions match the data. A non-trivial counterexample.

oeis-a326781.note: This disproves Barker's recurrence a(n) = a(n-1) + a(n-16) - a(n-17) at n=2049. a(2048)=32628 and a(2049)=65536, because bit 15 (position 16) is forbidden; I confirmed the first failures 2049, 2065, ... in Python. The formalization (positions counted from 1) is faithful. An obvious structural counterexample, routine.

oeis-a333794.note: Karttunen's conjecture (checked to 2^24) is that the gpf step is an optimal first step for the max path sum. The proof is a short exchange argument: for q < P = gpf(n), the q-step and P-step commute and gpf(n - n/q) = P, then strong induction. The formalization via fuelled recursion matches the data. Short but genuine.

oeis-a339532.note: Wu's recurrence and g.f. The Wieferich conditions for 2, 3, 5 are congruence conditions mod 4, 9, 25, so the set is a union of residue classes mod 900 minus b=1. That gives 8 terms per period, which is exactly the recurrence. Routine.

oeis-a353138.note: The fixed points of sum (#digits)^digit are only 1 and 4624. A bound (L <= 11 digits) plus an exhaustive kernel check over digit-count vectors. A finite check, routine.

oeis-a366860.note: The slope (sqrt(21)-3)/2 for the nested recurrence a(n) = n - a(floor(a(n-1)/3)). The formal statement includes the continued-fraction limit and the ratio limit. The proof uses strong induction with an O(sqrt n) error bound and a contraction of the two-level CF map. No earlier proof in the entry (revised Nov 9 2026). A modest but genuine analysis.

oeis-a372313.note: If A(n,1) == A(n,k-1) == 33 mod 100, their sum is 66 mod 100, so v2 = 1 and A372289 gives 2x+1 == 33 mod 100. A one-line induction. Trivial.

oeis-a374416.note: The statement matches 'a(n)=0 iff n=23' (practical number plus two nonagonal numbers k(7k-5)/2, k>=0). Somu-Tran (2024) proved representability only for sufficiently large n. The 129 KB proof gives an explicit construction at every scale (D q practical for D=2^t; nonagonal residues chosen mod D) plus kernel tables up to 8192. A complete, effective resolution; substantive.

oeis-a390007.note: Rodrigo's uniqueness of the minimum-defect 3-rectangle Mondrian partition except n=4. The two normal forms (three strips, or one strip plus a perpendicular split) are justified, and the encoding identifies congruent sets correctly. The proof is an elementary case analysis over these families. No earlier proof found.

mo-204379.note: The asker conjectured, from numerics, that the Jensen gap D(a;b) has a single maximum in a > 0. The formal statement asserts a unique global maximiser for any positive b that is not constant, with D defined exactly as in the question. The question (2015) has no answers, and the comments only discuss bounds. The proof writes D'(a) as a/(a+m)^3 times a weighted sum of strictly decreasing slope functions, so D' changes sign exactly once. This is a genuine (if elementary) argument, not a finite check.

oeis-a000657.note: Bala's May 2023 conjecture: median Euler numbers mod k are eventually periodic with period dividing phi(k). The Entringer-row definition reproduces the data (1,1,4,46,1024,36976,...), and the statement says exactly 'eventually periodic, period | phi(m)'. The entry still lists it as a conjecture, and I found no proof. The proof builds a finite-difference representation of the Entringer central values and applies Euler's theorem in each prime power. That takes a real idea, though the method is standard.

oeis-a005994.note: Mathar's 2025 conjecture a(n)+a(n+1) = A203286(n+1). I brute-forced the Configuration encoding (equal numbers of positive and negative entries, zero sum, at most n nonzero pairs), and it reproduces A203286 (4,12,28,57,...). The alkane formula reproduces A005994, and the identity checks for n <= 8. The proof is a bijective slice count. Routine.

oeis-a020964.note: Wu's Sep 2026 recurrence (n > 6) and g.f. The tsum definition with k+1 matches the entry (offset 0, data 1,4,11,28,...), and I checked that the recurrence holds for n >= 7 (it fails at n = 6, as the bound requires). The normalised g.f. reproduces the data. The proof shows the sum is finite and uses the silver-ratio trace recursion with a period-2 parity correction. A routine recurrence/g.f. identity.

oeis-a034108.note: Wu's 2024 recurrence (n > 8) and g.f. for the run starts of sqrt(m) whose first decimal is 2. The statement's digit and run-start encoding reproduces the data (5,18,28,39,...). I checked the recurrence and the g.f. for about 400 terms. The run starts are ceil((k+0.2)^2) for k = 2 and k >= 4, a quasi-polynomial of period 5. Routine.

oeis-a048331.note: Mathar's 2015 g.f. and recurrence a(n) = 7a(n-5) - 6a(n-10) for the base-6 repdigits, with a(0) = 0 included as in the entry. I checked the definition against the data and verified both identities numerically. The terms are d*(6^k-1)/5, so this is a routine g.f. identity.

oeis-a054117.note: This is Mathar's 2013 recurrence a(n) - (n+1)a(n-1) + n a(n-2) = 0. The row-sum construction of A054115 reproduces the data (1,6,30,150,870,...). I checked that the recurrence holds for 5 <= n <= 19 and fails only at n = 4 (left side 4). The statement file says so and restricts to n >= 5, which is the usual 'sufficiently large n' reading of Mathar's recurrences. The proof is a short telescoping of the double sums. Routine.

oeis-a057923.note: This is Israel's 2017 conjecture a(n+2) > a(n) for the greedy sequence that makes the pairwise ORs strictly increasing. The pick/pair encoding reproduces all 63 data terms, and the claim holds for 300 terms. The proof is a 50-line bitwise argument (y + ldiff x y = y OR x). Routine. Git history is squashed; the PR number is the later of the two merged PRs titled oeis-a057923, and #6867 is presumably the statement.

oeis-a071286.note: This is Barker's 2017 conjecture that the order-5 Peirce denominators are periodic with period 15 (the g.f. with denominator 1-x^15). I simulated the statement's token-stream insertion rule, and it reproduces the entry's data (2,4,5,3,1,5,4,3,5,4,2,5,3,4,5,...). The proof shows the insertion map preserves periodicity. This is the same routine pattern as A071284 in an earlier batch. Git history is squashed; the PR is the later of the two merged oeis-a071286 PRs.

oeis-a123341.note: Adams-Watters' 2006 conjecture that lim a(n)/2^n exists and is positive, where a(n) = sum_{k<=pi(n)} a(n-k). The definition reproduces the data (1,1,2,3,6,11,22,...). The entry and a web search show no proof. The proof shows that b(n) = a(n)/2^n satisfies b(n+1) >= b(n)(1 - 2^{-pi(n)}) and b(n+1) <= b(n). Since sum 2^{-pi(n)} converges (via a Chebyshev-type bound), the limit exists and is positive. Short, but a genuine analytic argument.

oeis-a127769.note: Mathar's 2014 recurrence for 3*C(4n-2,2n)/(2n+1), n > 1. The 'term' encoding is exactly a(k+1) = 3(4k+2)!/((2k+3)!(2k)!), and the recurrence is instantiated at n = t+2. The proof is field_simp and ring on factorials. A routine hypergeometric identity.

oeis-a141351.note: Mathar's 2014 P-recurrence for Catalan(n) + 1 - 0^n. The statement restricts to n >= 4 because at n = 3 the 0^n correction gives left side 2, which I confirmed. The recurrence holds for n = 4..39. The proof uses (j+2)C(j+1) = 2(2j+1)C(j) and ring. A routine identity.

oeis-a164008.note: Mathar's 2010 conjecture: row 8 of A163280 equals n(n+7) for n > 9. I recomputed the array from the statement's lowerDiv/Nat.nth encoding. It reproduces the data (0,17,34,39,68,65,102,98,...) and n(n+7) holds for 10 <= n < 190. The proof characterises the small elements of each column. Elementary and routine.

oeis-a175784.note: Mathar's 2010 conjectures: a(n) = 4*A060791(n+2), a(n) = 2a(n-5) - a(n-10), and the g.f. All three are stated, with the reduced-numerator definition (data 12,16,4,24,...), and I checked all three numerically. Since (2n-1)/(2n+9) + 1 = 4(n+2)/(2n+9) and gcd(4(n+2), 2n+9) = gcd(n+2, 5), everything follows from 5-periodicity. Routine.

oeis-a178299.note: Mathar's 2010 closed form a(n) = 3*8^n + 3*10^n/2 - 5*6^n + 12^n/2 for collinear 4-point subsets of {0..5}^n. The Finset/Collinear encoding counts unordered 4-sets, matching a(1) = 15 = C(6,4), a(2) = 234 and a(3) = 2820. The 1200-line proof is a standard double count: a collinear 4-set has step 3, 4 or 5 along its line, with a 2-to-1 parameterisation. Long, but routine combinatorics. I found no earlier proof.

oeis-a191993.note: Mathar's 2017 P-recurrence for 3^(n-1) + C(2n,n)/2, instantiated at n = t+3. Over Q the definition matches the data (2,6,19,62,207,...), and the recurrence holds for n >= 3. The proof is the central-binomial step and ring. Routine.

oeis-a192745.note: Mathar's 2014 recurrence for the x-coefficient of p(n,x) mod x^2-x-1, where p(n,x) = x p(n-1,x) + n!. The modByMonic encoding reproduces the data (0,1,2,5,13,42,175,...), and the recurrence holds for n = 3..29. The proof shows the combination is a multiple of x^2-x-1 plus a constant. Routine.

oeis-a192942.note: Mathar's 2014 recurrence for the x-coefficient of (2x+1)...(2x+n) mod x^2-x-1. The encoding reproduces the data (0,2,10,62,448,...), and the recurrence holds for n = 2..29. The proof tracks the 2-dimensional coordinates of the reduction and eliminates one of them. Routine.

oeis-a199705.note: Barker's 2018 g.f. and parity closed forms for zero-sum triples in -n..n with no equal neighbours. The Finset filter reproduces the data (6,14,32,52,82,...), and both parity formulas and the g.f. check numerically. The proof counts fibres over the middle entry. Routine.

oeis-a227721.note: Kimberling's 2013 conjecture floor(1/s(n)) = 6n^2+9n+2 (plus the induced cubic recurrence), with s(n) = (2n+1)/(2n+2) - n log((n+1)/n). The definition matches the entry, and I checked the closed form in 60-digit arithmetic for n < 300. The proof brackets log(1+1/n) with the atanh series in y = 1/(2n+1), showing 1/s(n) lies in [6n^2+9n+2, 6n^2+9n+3). Standard series estimates, so routine.

oeis-a233579.note: Kaarhus's 2013 conjecture: den(B_n)/6 mod 30 is in {11,17,23,25,29} iff |num(B_n)| == 5 (mod 6). The statement covers all n, and odd n and n <= 1 are handled correctly. I checked the equivalence for n <= 260 with exact Bernoulli numbers. It follows from von Staudt-Clausen: num == -den/2 (mod 2) and -den/3 (mod 3), and the sign of B_2k is tied to whether 5 | den. A short consequence of classical theorems. Routine.

oeis-a243513.note: Barker's 2018 closed form 4a(n) = 7 + 3^n + 2n and g.f. for Hardin's restricted-growth words avoiding aba/abb. The validWord encoding (each nonzero value preceded by its predecessor; consecutive-triple condition) is the restricted-growth condition. A brute force for n <= 6 reproduces the data and the formula. The proof splits by maximum value. Routine.

oeis-a248183.note: Oudra's 2023 conjecture a(n) = floor(sqrt(n^2/2+1) - 1/2) for n > 1, stated with the equivalent integer square root form (isqrt(2n^2+4)-1)/2. The tail telescopes to 1/(2(k+1)(k+2)), so the claim is a quadratic inequality. I checked it by brute force for n < 120. Routine.

oeis-a253975.note: Ratushnyak's 2015 conjecture that no term is -1, i.e. for every n some k has exactly n representations x*y+x+y with x >= y > 1. The statement (Fin n equivalent to the representations of k) is that existence claim. The proof takes k = 3^(2n+1) - 1: then (x+1)(y+1) = 3^(2n+1) has exactly n factorisations with y+1 = 3^j, 1 <= j <= n. Trivial.

oeis-a259775.note: Mathar's 2015 P-recurrence for the stepped path through iterated partial sums of squares. The partialSums/path encoding reproduces the data (1,5,6,20,27,77,112,...), and the recurrence (at n = t+4) checks exactly for 26 shifts. The proof finds the closed form (2j+r+2)(j+r+1)!/((r+2)! j!) and verifies a rational identity. Routine.

oeis-a262999.note: Sun's 2015 conjecture says a(n) = 1 only for n in {3,5,7,35,37,217,7439,10381}. The statement adds 590, because the entry's own example has a(590) = 1. That weakens the claim, so a disproof of it refutes Sun's version too. The disproof shows a(7872413) = 1 with the single pair (15015, 4749). I reproduced this with an independent numpy sieve to 1.39e8: pi(112732620) = 6450605, pi(22553001) = 1421808, and exactly one representation. Sun had checked only to 120000, and I found no earlier report. A computational counterexample, so routine.

oeis-a266438.note: De Vlieger's g.f. and Barker's closed form and recurrence for the cumulative ON cells of Rule 23. The background evolves as in the entry's program, which I simulated: it reproduces the data (1,4,4,11,11,22,...) and both formulas for n <= 40. The proof uses the rule 'ON iff at most one neighbour is ON', which gives an eventually periodic pattern. Routine, like the other Barker CA items in earlier batches.

oeis-a266795.note: Barker's closed form (n > 3), recurrence (n > 8) and g.f. for the cumulative OFF cells of Rule 61, with the background evolving. My simulation reproduces the data (0,1,4,6,11,15,23,...) and both formulas in their stated ranges. An eventually periodic CA pattern. Routine.

oeis-a267923.note: Barker's recurrence a(n) = 101a(n-1) - 100a(n-2) (n > 2) and g.f. for the Rule 245 rows read in base 10. The background evolves (000 -> ON) as in the entry's program, which I simulated: it gives 1, 11, 11011, 1111011, ..., and the recurrence holds for n = 3..30. The proof shows row n is ON everywhere except cell n-2. Routine.

oeis-a276646.note: Krizek's 2016 conjecture that (sum_{k<=n} 0.k)/n <= 0.55. The exact decimalFraction k/10^(len k) is the source's 0.k. In exact arithmetic the mean stays below 0.55 up to n = 2*10^5, approaching it at n = 10^d - 1 (0.549977...). The proof is an elementary block-by-block arithmetic-progression bound. Routine. Git history is squashed; the PR is the later merged oeis-a276646 PR.

oeis-a306571.note: The disproof refutes Sun's 2019 conjecture that every n is w(w+1) + C(x+3,4) + C(y+5,6) + C(z+7,8). The counterexample is n = 41215718, which has no representation. Sun had checked n up to 2*10^7. I confirmed with an independent brute force that a(41215718) = 0, a(41215717) = 15 and a(41215719) = 44, as the certificate states. The definition reproduces the 101 data terms. I found no earlier report of this counterexample. A computational disproof (finite check), so routine, but a genuine new refutation.

oeis-a330080.note: Cicuttin's 2019 conjecture 0 <= floor(b(n)) <= 5 for b(n) = (b(n-1)+b(n-2))/b(n-3) with b(1) = b(2) = b(3) = 1. The proof uses the conserved quantity (1+x)(1+y)(1+z)(x+y+z)/(xyz) = 24 of this third-order Lyness-type map, which is classical (Cima-Gasull-Manosa), and a polynomial inequality showing every term is below 6. No proof is in the entry. Routine given the known invariant.

oeis-a366870.note: Gutkovskiy's 2023 conjecture a(n) ~ 2(sqrt 2 - 1) n for a(n) = n - a(floor(a(n-1)/4)), a Hofstadter-G variant. The definition and the continued-fraction limit match the entry. The entry and its siblings (denominators 3 and 5) still list it as a conjecture, and I found no proof. The proof bounds the error from the linear slope by 16 sqrt(n) by strong induction, for any denominator >= 3, using contraction of the two-level continued-fraction map. A genuine asymptotic argument.

oeis-a372430.note: The disproof refutes Wiseman's 2024 conjecture that 4100 is the only k whose binary indices are a subset of its prime indices (verified only to 10^7). The counterexample is k = 2^87 + 2^49 = 154742504911235484315811840. Its binary indices are {50, 88}, and I checked that prime(50) = 229 and prime(88) = 457 both divide it. The encoding (1-based bit positions, prime(1) = 2) matches the entry's example 4100. No earlier report found. An explicit computational counterexample, so routine, but a genuine new refutation.

oeis-a375583.note: The conjecture (checked to 10^8) is that 11 is the only n that is not a practical number plus two 11-gonal numbers. Somu-Tran (JIS 2024, Thm 2) prove this only for n > N(s), with an astronomically large, never-computed N(s), so the conjecture was open. The definitions (practical number; k(9k-7)/2, k >= 0) are faithful. The 900-line proof gives an explicit construction at every scale: Dq is practical for D = 2^t and q <= 2D, and the polygonal residues are chosen mod D = BL, plus a finite check. A substantive effectivisation. Git history is squashed; the PR is the later merged oeis-a375583 PR.

oeis-a382624.note: Xausa's 2025 conjecture that A382621 (lexicographically earliest digit-stream sequence) sorted is A382624. The greedy state with seed 9 and the least-unused rule reproduce A382621's opening (1,3,2,5,4,7,6,9,8,10,...). The statement says this sequence is injective with image exactly the admissible numbers. The proof uses that all-nines repunits can follow anything, so every admissible number is eventually used. Routine.

oeis-a390815.note: Dequatre's two Feb 2026 conjectures: every reduced denominator > 1 of n!/sigma(n) is prime, and for n >= 4, sigma(n) not dividing n! forces n to be a square. Both are stated faithfully. The proof is elementary. If n is not a prime power, sigma(n) | n! by multiplicativity. If n = p^k, sigma(n) < 2n, so it divides n! or is a prime > n, and for odd k, (1+p) | sigma(n) rules the latter out. Routine.

oeis-a301517.note: Lagneau's 2018 conjecture: if (sum of nonsquarefree divisors)/(sum of squarefree divisors) is a perfect square, it is the square of a prime. The statement is faithful (k>0, ratio k^2 implies k prime). PR #7662 disproved it with root 3107; the merged file (#10580) uses n = 19773000 = 2^3*3^2*5^3*13^3, where I recomputed the sums 1008 and 72398592, ratio 71824 = 268^2 with 268 composite. The entry has no prior counterexample. It is a finite certificate.

oeis-a330408.note: Sada's conjecture that the diagonal of the least-multiple table is A166447 = n*round(sqrt n). The table definition reproduces the entry's antidiagonals. I recomputed A(19,19) = 95 (19 -> 20 -> 21 -> 24 -> 25 -> 30 -> ... -> 95) against A166447(19) = 76, so the claim first fails at n = 19. The entry has no earlier correction. A finite counterexample.

oeis-a334765.note: Konig's 2020 conjecture: no four consecutive terms (binary weight = minus the balanced-ternary digit sum). The extra conjuncts restate the comment's data (first run 32770..32772, 115 earlier terms) and are finite checks. The core is a short parity argument. For n not 1 mod 3 the ternary sum goes up by 1, so the binary weight must drop by 1, which forces n = 3 mod 4. Two of three consecutive n would both need this, which is impossible. Not in the entry.

oeis-a000267.note: Karttunen's conjecture A070939(A227368(n+1)) = floor(sqrt(4n+1)). I checked that the formal run-length decoder reproduces A227183 and its first-occurrence codes reproduce A227368, and that the identity holds for n<60. The proof is an elementary extremal argument: the largest partition encodable in L bits has size floor((L+1)^2/4), from balanced rectangles. Not settled in the entry.

oeis-a058764.note: Hasler's conjecture: the least x with x - phi(x) = 2^n is 3*2^(n-1) for n>1. The entry gives only the upper bound (Mathar). The proof writes x = 2^a m and shows that 2m - phi(m) can be a power of 2 with m>1 only when phi(m) is 2 mod 4. That makes m a prime power p^k with p = 3 mod 4, so phi(m)/m >= 2/3. A short elementary argument.

oeis-a076902.note: Cloitre's |a(n) - n/3| < log(n+1) plus a(n) ~ n/3. The definition matches the data (checked). With e(n) = a(n) - n/3, |e(n)| <= 1/3 + |e(n/2)|, so |e(n)| <= (1/3)log2(n) + O(1), well below ln(n+1). Routine.

oeis-a108475.note: Mathar's a(n) = Pell(n+1)*A001333(n) for the coefficients of (1-3x)/(1-5x-5x^2+x^3). The definitions match the data (checked). A product of two C-finite sequences: a routine identity (10-line proof).

oeis-a124870.note: Barker's a(n) = 2500a(n-4) for n>6 and his g.f. for the denominators of Re((3i-1)^-n). The formal base is exactly 1/(-1+3i) and reproduces the data. Routine: it follows from the 2- and 5-adic valuations of Re((-1-3i)^n).

oeis-a127771.note: Barry's conjecture that the inverse of the triangle 1/phi(n+1)[k<=n<=2k] is integral, stated for every finite truncation (equivalent). Trivial: the matrix is D*B with D = diag(1/phi(n+1)) and B a 0-1 unitriangular integer matrix, so the inverse B^-1 D^-1 has entries B^-1(n,k)*phi(k+1).

oeis-a134347.note: Werner's closed form for the inverse binomial transform of A134346(n,k) = (2^(n+1)-1)C(n,k). The definitions reproduce the data (checked). A routine binomial-sum identity.

oeis-a141353.note: Mathar's recurrence for Catalan(n) + 2^n - 0^n. It is stated for n>=4 because at n=3 the 0^n correction gives 8, not 0 (a correct, documented range choice). A routine holonomic identity.

oeis-a164011.note: Mathar's T(11,n) = n(n+10) for n>20. The definition reproduces the data (checked). Elementary: for k>20 the 11 smallest j with largest divisor <= sqrt(j) equal to k are k(k+i), i=0..10, since k+j | k(k+i) needs k+j <= j(i-j) <= 25.

oeis-a178351.note: Mathar's closed form 2*11^n + 13^n/2 + 5*9^n - 15*7^n/2 for collinear 5-subsets of {0..6}^n, with real collinearity. The closed form gives 0, 21, 364, 4833, as in the data. A long but routine line-classification count (same type as A178297/A178298 in earlier batches).

oeis-a192357.note: Barker's order-4 recurrence for the constant term of p(n-1,x) mod x^2-x-1. The definition reproduces the data with offset 1 (checked). A routine C-finite identity.

oeis-a192752.note: Mathar's closed form via A000071. The polynomial recursion p(n) = x p(n-1) + 4n+3 reproduces the data (checked). Routine.

oeis-a207262.note: Ianakiev's sigma_m(m)/sigma_m^odd(m) = 2^m+1 for m = 4n-2. Faithful (cross-multiplied). Trivial: m = 2*odd, so the divisors are the odd d and 2d.

oeis-a233656.note: Forberg's period-20 pattern of last digits, with equal frequencies. The recurrence matches the data (checked). A finite check of the recurrence mod 10 (with n mod 20).

oeis-a259914.note: Mathar's order-3 P-recurrence for the staircase path through iterated partial sums of cubes. The path definition reproduces the data (checked, offset 1). A routine holonomic identity.

oeis-a265430.note: Barker's closed form, recurrence and g.f. for the OFF cells of Rule 188. I re-simulated the formal automaton (background evolving), which matches the data. The pattern is eventually periodic: routine.

oeis-a266450.note: Barker's formulas for the cumulative OFF cells of Rule 25. The simulation matches the data and the closed form for n>2. Routine CA pattern verification.

oeis-a266844.note: Barker's formulas for the Rule 70 rows read in base 10. The simulation matches the data and 198a(n) = 209*100^n - 9(-100)^n - 2*10^n. Routine.

oeis-a267941.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. for the Rule 253 rows in binary. The simulation (background turns ON) matches the data, and a(n) = 2^(2n+1)-1 for n>1. Routine.

oeis-a306948.note: Mathar's D-finite recurrence for the e.g.f. (1+x)log(1+x)e^x, stated for n>=4. A routine holonomic verification.

oeis-a345096.note: Kotesovec's a(n) ~ n^2/2. The definition matches the data (checked). The summand is k if k^i | n and 1 otherwise, so a(n) = n(n+1)/2 + O(sigma(n) log n). Routine.

oeis-a367191.note: The mod-4 formulas for the largest k with k^2+kn+n^2 square, for n>=1 (n=0 is excluded correctly). I checked them against a divisor-based exact computation for n<3000. Elementary: (2m-2k-n)(2m+2k+n) = 3n^2, so take the smallest admissible factor.

oeis-a376868.note: Greathouse's 'conjecturally the sum of permanents of all n X n 0-1 matrices' equals n!*4^C(n,2). Faithful. A one-line double count: each permutation's diagonal is all ones in 2^(n^2-n) matrices.

oeis-a383062.note: Xausa's conjecture that A383059 is a permutation of the admissible numbers A383062. I simulated the formal greedy, which reproduces A383059's data. The proof uses 'bridge' numbers 2*10^j, which can follow anything and be followed by anything, to show that every admissible number is eventually chosen. A short standard argument.

oeis-a386969.note: McEachen's parity formulas and He's g.f. for this Recaman variant. The formal recursion matches the data, and both claims hold through n=400 (checked). An inductive eventually-periodic pattern: routine.

mo-319325.note: Unanswered 2018 question: does P_n^{-1/2} X_n P_n^{-1/2} always converge when P_n -> Pbar singular? The formalization (Hurwitz A, PD X_n and P_n solving the Lyapunov equation, PSD limits, det Pbar = 0) is faithful. The disproof uses A = [[-1,1],[0,-1]] and P_k = diag(s^2,t^2) with t/s alternating between 1 and 3/2. The normalized off-diagonal entry is -t/s, which oscillates, and X_k is PD since t < 2s (I checked).
