oeis-a202253.note: Kimberling's closed form 1+2*floor((2n^2+2n)/3) for Hardin's count of zero-sum triples in -n..n with bounded adjacent differences. The definition is faithful, controls a(1..6) match, and the proof is a direct residue-class count. Routine.

oeis-a297443.note: Kimberling's conjecture that the recurrence sequence gives the least positive integer with base-3 total variation n is stated faithfully. Total variation is the sum of |differences| of consecutive digits, matching A297440, and the controls match the data. The proof is an elementary digit-extremal argument with explicit lower-bound tables. Routine.

oeis-a321612.note: The statement (exactly {2,4,6,7,9,13,16,21,31} qualify) faithfully encodes 'all triangular t with k/2 <= t < k have k-t triangular', with the nonemptiness condition implicit in the data. I re-checked the definition numerically up to 20000. The finiteness proof is a short gap argument about adjacent triangular numbers near the midpoint. Routine.

oeis-a308159.note: Barker's g.f. and recurrence for the sum of largest sides of isosceles integer triangles with perimeter n. The definition reproduces the data (controls a(0..11)). The proof is a closed form plus a g.f. identity. Routine.

oeis-a232867.note: Kimberling's conjectured quadratic formula, g.f. and recurrence for the positions of -n in the x+1 / i*x tree. The Mathematica DeleteDuplicates construction is modelled faithfully and controls a(1..4) match. The proof analyses distance generations and counts. Routine.

oeis-a286807.note: The conjecture that the n-th iterate of 00->001, 1->101 (StringReplace semantics) has A132045(n) letters is stated faithfully, with controls for the listed iterates. The proof is a token recoding and induction. Routine.

oeis-a390208.note: The conjectured g.f. (1/3)(prod 1/(1-x^j)^3 - prod 1/(1-x^{3j})) for partitions with parts coloured {0,1,2} and colour sum ≡ 1 mod 3 is stated coefficientwise with truncated geometric series, which is faithful. It is an immediate roots-of-unity filter: F(omega) = prod 1/(1-x^{3j}) and omega+omega^2 = -1. Routine.

oeis-a086524.note: Murthy's conjecture (every prime ≡ 5 mod 6 is the mean of two successive terms of A086523) is disproved with p = 17. The greedy model of A086523 reproduces its data (5,17,29,53,41,...). All terms are ≡ 5 mod 12, so the only possible pair is (5,29), and 5 and 29 are not adjacent. The entry flagged no counterexample, though A086523 had a parallel refutation in 2008. A trivial disproof.

oeis-a377112.note: Kimberling's conjecture (every prime divides infinitely many a(n), with eventually periodic gaps) is stated faithfully via the 4x4 integer step on coefficients of 1, sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt6, with a real-identity control. The proof shows the reduction mod p is eventually periodic, using the adjugate identity adj*step = -23*I. Routine.

oeis-a249968.note: Wu's conjecture that squares of terms end in 00 or 56 is stated faithfully. wrap(m) = 2*10^(d+2)+100m+25, with controls 16 and 14130. The proof is a short modular analysis (83 lines). Routine.

oeis-a269876.note: Barker's five conjectured formulas for the 2D outer-totalistic Rule 43 automaton. The rule bit s+2k, the plane evolution and the count on [-n,n]^2 follow the entry's program, and controls match. The proof describes the explicit stage patterns and counts. Routine.

oeis-a273443.note: Barker's closed form 4n(n+1) for n > 3, the recurrence and the g.f. for 2D Rule 721. The definition matches the entry's conventions, and controls 1,4,21,41,80,120,168,224 match. Explicit stage description. Routine.

oeis-a063656.note: Lowell's greedy characterization (a(n) is the least number > a(n-1) that is a square iff n is triangular) is stated faithfully. The terms are where floor(sqrt k) = round(sqrt k), with offset 0 and controls. Elementary. Routine.

oeis-a358696.note: Manyama's order-9 recurrence for boundary-covering cycles in the 5 x n grid. The cycle is an edge set that is connected, 2-regular and covers all boundary vertices, matching the definition. The proof is a certified transfer-matrix computation with a polynomial annihilator. Routine (finite linear algebra).

oeis-a203164.note: Mathar's recurrence a(n) = 48a(n-4) - 576a(n-8) and g.f. for e_{n-1} of the periodic sequence (4,1,2,3,...). I checked that the definition reproduces the data 1,5,14,50,224,... and the recurrence numerically. Routine.

oeis-a090413.note: Mathar's holonomic recurrence for the Chebyshev transform of 3^n, defined directly from the entry's g.f. via the Catalan series substitution. A standard D-finite verification of an algebraic g.f. Routine.

oeis-a329178.note: Barker's g.f. and recurrence for partial sums of Padovan(i+5)*Padovan(i+7) (A000931 indexing). The data offset is consistent. Routine linear-recurrence identity.

oeis-a046385.note: Pfoertner's conjecture (the sequence has no terms beyond the 17 recorded) is disproved by an explicit 79-digit palindrome: 2977792 * P, where P is a sparse palindromic prime certified by Pocklington. It has exactly 14 palindromic prime factors (2^12 * 727 * P), so a(14) exists and is not in the list. I verified the palindrome, primality and factorization in Python. Consistent with the entry's remark that other terms would need >= 18 digits. An explicit certificate.

oeis-a266982.note: Hurt's divisor-sum parity formula for the Rule 81 triangle. The automaton is run on the full line, rows are read -t..t, and indexing starts at t^2, which matches the entry. The proof describes the CA explicitly and uses the hyperbola parity of sum floor((n-2)/i). Routine.

oeis-a060765.note: Corneth's conjecture (if consecutive-divisor differences all divide n, then p-1 | n/p for every prime p | n) is stated faithfully with an explicit consecutiveness condition. The proof is a short elementary divisor argument (about 70 lines). Routine.

oeis-a004215.note: Neumann's count conjecture (#{m < 2^n in A004215} = A023105(n) - 2 for n >= 1) is stated faithfully. Membership is defined literally, and A023105 is the number of squares mod 2^n. Given Legendre's three-square theorem (the terms are 4^a(8b+7)), this is a direct count. The proof formalizes Legendre via Ankeny's argument, but the mathematical content beyond the classical theorem is routine.

oeis-a366871.note: The asymptotic a(n) ~ ((3sqrt5-5)/2) n for a(n) = n - a(floor(a(n-1)/5)) is stated over every function satisfying the recurrence, which determines it uniquely. The proof is a short strong induction giving |a(n) - cn| <= 10 sqrt(n), using c^2 + 5c = 5. Routine.

oeis-a067576.note: Kimberling's conjecture says each column of T+1 is eventually geometric with ratio 2. The statement proves the stronger exact start row max(1,j) for column j+1, which agrees with his d(1..5) = 1,1,2,3,4. Rows are the numbers with i set bits, which is the same as 2^i || C(2m,m) by Kummer. Explicit formula 2^(i+1)-1-2^(i-j). Routine.

oeis-a341239.note: The conjecture 1 < r s n - floor(r floor(s n)) < 3 with r = 1+sqrt2 and s = sqrt2 is stated faithfully. It follows directly from floor bounds and the irrationality of sqrt2. Routine.

oeis-a269454.note: For distinct safe primes p, q not ≡ -1 mod 8, ord_{pq}(2) = phi(pq)/2. Such p are 5 or ≡ 3 mod 8, so 2 is a non-residue and ord_p(2) = p-1, and gcd(p-1, q-1) = 2 gives the lcm. Faithful and routine.

oeis-a394678.note: If (n!-1) mod n^2 is prime (n != 4), then n and n^2-n-1 are prime. The entry already notes, via Wilson, that a(p) = p^2-p-1 for prime p. The remaining composite case is trivial: n^2 | n! for composite n != 4, so a(n) = n^2-1 is composite. Faithful and routine.

oeis-a266072.note: Barker's closed form and recurrence and De Vlieger's g.f. for elementary Rule 3, counted on sites -n..n with the background evolving. These match the data 1,1,1,5,1,9,... Explicit description. Routine.

oeis-a362069.note: Petrescu's conjecture (infinitely many consecutive pairs k, k+1 with k + digitsum(k^2) square) is stated faithfully. The proof is an explicit infinite family built by padding with powers of ten. Short construction. Routine.

oeis-a044279.note: Dale's digit-sum conjecture for numbers whose base-9 form contains 31 but whose predecessor's does not. The statement encodes this exactly, with Mathlib's LSB-first digits (so [1,3] means '31'). The proof uses decimal digit sum ≡ k mod 9 and the structure of the first numbers in each block. Routine.

oeis-a180195.note: Mathar's D-finite recurrence for the alternating sum of (j-1)!(j^2-j+1), stated within the offset. Routine telescoping.

oeis-a083137.note: The conjecture that the greedy coprime-palindrome sequence is infinite is stated as the existence of a full greedy sequence. The proof uses the palindromes 10^((M+1)!)+1, which are coprime to every b <= M, so a candidate always exists. Routine.

oeis-a134799.note: Finch's conjecture that the reduced denominator of the Newton iterate b(n) for 1/sqrt3 is 3^((3^n+1)/2) = 3*A134799(n). The proof is a 3-adic valuation induction. Routine.

oeis-a394454.note: Both claims (every prime divides C(2n,n) for infinitely many n, and the sum of distinct prime divisors is unbounded) follow at once from Kummer/Legendre and from primes in (n,2n]. Faithful and trivial.

oeis-a263805.note: Barker's recurrence and g.f. and Keller's parity closed forms for the Rule 157 rows read as base-10 numbers. The automaton runs on the full line with the background evolving, and the definition reproduces the listed terms. Explicit row description. Routine.

oeis-a216971.note: Perry's 2012 conjecture says every entry T(n,k) (endofunctions of [n] with exactly k non-recurrent points mapped directly into cycles) is divisible by n. The statement is faithful: periodic points are the recurrent ones, and k ranges over 0..n-1. Divisibility is not apparent from Critzer's e.g.f., and the proof is a combinatorial argument (about 470 lines). I found no earlier proof. Moderate rather than deep.

oeis-a387471.note: The conjectured closed form for interior triple concurrences of equal-angle cevians in an equilateral triangle (m = 2n-1) is stated via trigonometric Ceva. d(m) counts ordered triples (i,j,k) with prod sin x/sin(pi/3-x) = 1, x = (i+1)pi/(3(m+1)), which matches the entry's R-function formulation, and each concurrency point has at most one cevian per vertex. The entry calls the formula conjectural (verified n <= 200). The proof classifies the solutions with a roots-of-unity bound on rational relations among six terms, in the spirit of Conway–Jones and Poonen–Rubinstein. Substantive. I found no earlier derivation of this count.

oeis-a374365.note: Granvik's 2024 conjecture: m is a term iff m has a prime factor = 1 mod 10. The statement uses the principal complex power (-1)^(2k/5) = zeta_5^k, exactly as the entry's Mathematica program does, with offset m>=1. Since primes = 1 mod 5 are odd, 'p = 1 mod 10' is the same as 'p = 1 mod 5'. The proof is short but genuine: an involution d <-> dp cancels the sum when such a p divides m, and otherwise linear independence of the powers of zeta_5 forces sum mu(d) d = prod(1-p) = 0 in Z/5, which is impossible. I found no earlier proof.

oeis-a057566.note: The floor formula (as corrected by Alper Ferudun, Oct 2026) is faithfully stated for n>=1 with Fin 3 x Fin n and the zero-cross-product test. Collinear triples are the 3*C(n,3) vertical ones plus one point per column in arithmetic progression, so a(n)=n^3/2-n^2+n+(1-(-1)^n)/4, which is already in the entry (Mathar 2010); the floor identity follows. Routine count.

oeis-a002791.note: Irvine's 2014 formula a(n)=4 sigma(n)-f(n mod 6). 4sigma(n)-a(n)=sum_{d|n,d<=4} d(4-d)=3+4[2|n]+3[3|n], which is f(n mod 6). One-line routine identity; statement faithful.

oeis-a274782.note: Bala's 2023 supercongruence a(np^r) = a(np^(r-1)) mod p^(2r), p >= 5. The statement defines a(n) by Bala's sum Sum C(n,k)C(n+k,k)C(k,n-k), which the entry derives from Eger's theorem; I checked it against all listed terms of the diagonal. The quantifiers match (n, r > 0, p >= 5 prime). The proof is substantial: a Legendre-type identity with a period-6 twist, plus Jacobsthal-Kazandzidis scaling. I found no earlier proof. General Dwork-crystal results (Mellit-Vlasenko, Beukers-Vlasenko) give only mod p^r here, and the October 2026 Bala-conjecture preprints (Blanco Gomez and others) do not list A274782.

oeis-a389591.note: Pol's conjectured identity a(n)=sigma(n)-A379379(n). The proof is a three-line case split: a divisor r is not counted in a(n) iff r=1 or r>2*prevdiv, iff r is odd with no divisor d satisfying d<r<2d. Routine.

oeis-a261681.note: Mathar's 2017 order-4 P-recurrence for 2^n+C(n,floor(n/2))-1, stated for n>=4 exactly as in the entry. The proof is a direct factorial computation split by parity. Routine holonomic identity.

oeis-a278415.note: Sun's 2016 conjecture that (a(pn)-a(n))/(pn)^2 is a p-adic integer for p > 3. The statement forms the quotient in Q and asks that p not divide its denominator, which is exactly p-integrality; the definition matches the data. The entry itself only claims the weaker (p^2 n) version. Pan-Sun (2026) proved the analogous conjectures for A277640 and A208425 but not this sequence, and I found no other proof. The proof file says it is an original argument.

oeis-a247727.note: Hardin's empirical polynomial n^4+2n^3+3n^2+2n plus Barker's recurrence and g.f. and Spezia's e.g.f. The reading of 'no disjoint pairs ... same sum' as the three pairings of a length-4 array matches the data. Inclusion-exclusion count, so routine.

oeis-a035378.note: Bala's 2023 mod-5 congruences for the expansion of Kontsevich's F(q) = Sum (q;q)_k about q = -1. Writing x = Y-1 and truncating at k <= 2n+1 is exact, because the k-th product is divisible by Y^floor(k/2); the first terms match the data. These congruences mirror the Andrews-Sellers / Garthwaite-Rhoades mod-5 congruences for Fishburn numbers (the expansion at q = 1). But Garvan, Ahlgren-Kim, Straub and Guerzhoy-Kent-Rolen all treat expansions at q = 1 (or F((1-q)^r)), not at q = -1. I found no earlier proof.

OeisA179524.conjecture3.note: The upstream statement (research open at the pinned commit) matches Sun's 2010 claim: Sum_{k<p} a(k) = 0 mod p^2 for p = 11,13,17,19 mod 20. Numerically this sum agrees mod p^2 with Sum C(2k,k)^2 C(4k,2k)/(-1024)^k. For that sum, Z.-H. Sun proved only the split case mod p (Legendre polynomials II, Thm 5.3), and his 2020 list still records the mod p^2 congruence as Z.-W. Sun's conjecture. I found no proof of either form before the PR. Some residual risk remains, because the Sun-conjecture literature is large.

oeis-a297402.note: Jackson's conjecture that the gcd over the first n odd primes equals the gcd over all odd primes. It is stated faithfully as initialGcd n | (p^n-1)/2 for every odd prime p (the reverse divisibility is automatic). Corneth's comments already show the gcd is a power of 2 and settle odd n. The even case is lifting-the-exponent with p = 3 among the first n primes. Routine.

oeis-a195334.note: Mathar's conjecture a(n) = 2*A023194(n). Odd k have even-divisor sum 0, and the even-divisor sum of 2m is 2*sigma(m), so the two sets correspond under k = 2m and Nat.nth matches. The statement is faithful (offset 1, Nat.nth at n-1). No prior public solution was found, but the argument is a two-line observation. Second review: Faithful and true. For odd k the even-divisor sum is 0, and for k=2m it is 2*sigma(m), so the two sets correspond by doubling, which preserves order. A one-line elementary argument, hence routine.

oeis-a247173.note: Mathar's conjectured D-finite recurrence. The power-series encoding (S^2 = P with S(0) = 1, and G*(2x^2+2x)*S = 1-3x^2-2x^3-S) determines G uniquely and matches the g.f. I checked the polynomial coefficients term by term against the entry. The proof derives an ODE from the algebraic g.f., the standard holonomic method. Second review: Faithful D-finite recurrence for an algebraic g.f.; true and checked. Standard holonomic-closure computation, hence routine.

arxiv-1804.09594.note: This is Kuca's Conjecture 3.1 (2018): for n = 2^k+1 >= 5, the even terms of V(2,n) are exactly 2, 2n and 2n^2+2. The Lean greedy definition (unordered, not necessarily distinct, exactly one representation) matches the paper, and I recomputed n = 5, 9, 17, 33 up to 40000 ([2,10,52], [2,18,164], [2,34,580], [2,66,2180]). No prior proof turned up on arXiv, Zenodo (the 2026 Funayama note covers only U-sequences), trureturing, thatnealpatel/proofs, openai/math or Palomar. The proof is a substantial 3277-line argument via Sierpinski-type dyadic rows, marked 'STATUS: NEW'. Second review: Faithful statement of Kuca's Conjecture 3.1; no prior resolution found. A 3277-line kernel-checked proof using Lucas/Sierpinski parity structure; a genuine new result, not routine.

oeis-a162481.note: Mathar's conjectured order-4 recurrence for c(x/(1-x)^3)/(1-x)^3. The encoding reproduces the data, and the recurrence holds on all listed terms (checked). This is a standard holonomic derivation from an algebraic g.f. Second review: Faithful and true; a routine D-finite recurrence derived from the quadratic g.f.

oeis-a129147.note: Mathar's conjectured recurrence for c(x(1+2x)). The encoding 2x(1+2x)G = 1-S with S^2 = 1-4x-8x^2 matches the data, and the recurrence holds on the data. The method is the routine holonomic one. Second review: Faithful and true; a routine D-finite recurrence from an algebraic g.f.

oeis-a085267.note: Greathouse's conjecture a(n) = n+11 for n > 50 (every m >= 62 has at least 2 representations as a nonzero square plus a squarefree number, and exactly 50 terms are <= 61). The statement is faithful (k > 0, n-k^2 squarefree, so >= 1). I confirmed it numerically to 2*10^5. The proof is a large but elementary sieve plus a kernel check below 1.2*10^7; I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful. The proof combines a kernel-checked sieve up to 1.2e7 with an explicit elementary sieve bound above that, which is a genuine effective version of Estermann. Jimenez Urroz's explicit paper proves the weaker one-representation, zero-square-allowed statement, so the claim does not appear to be already settled.

oeis-a391613.note: The conjecture is that every n > 5 equals x^2+y+z with x >= 1, y >= z >= 1 and lcm(x^2,y,z) a square. The statement is faithful and reproduces the data a(1..25); I checked n < 3000, and the entry reports n <= 150000. The 2651-line proof combines elementary square-scaling families with Legendre's three-square theorem (formalized via Ankeny), a Minkowski determinant-1 lemma, CRT and a genus pigeonhole step. No prior proof was found; the conjecture dates from Jan 2026. Second review: Faithful statement of a recent (Jan 2026) Sun conjecture with no recorded proof. Elementary (three-square theorem plus casework) but not a short argument from the entry, so not routine.

oeis-a060212.note: It disproves White's 2023 heuristic a(n) ~ n log n log(n log n) log log n. A Selberg upper-bound sieve gives #{q <= x} << x/log^3 x, which forces a(n) >> n log^3 n, incompatible with the conjectured order n log^2 n log log n; if the sequence is finite the equivalence fails trivially. The sieve code is reused, with credit, from site PR 2394 (Enamakel). This is a standard sieve argument against an obviously mis-scaled conjecture. Second review: A correct, unconditional disproof by a formalized Selberg upper-bound sieve. The sieve code is credited to PR 2394 from the same site, which is fine. The conjecture was heuristically implausible but never refuted in print; the disproof is standard analytic number theory, not routine.

oeis-a027116.note: Barker's order-5 recurrence for the triangle diagonal T(n,n+3) of A027113, for n > 7. The Lean triangle reproduces the OEIS data, and the recurrence holds numerically to n = 60. The proof expresses the diagonal through tribonacci numbers, a routine linear-recurrence verification. Second review: Faithful and true. The left part of each row is tribonacci (Pirc's comment), which makes a(n) a linear-recurrence sequence; a routine verification.

oeis-a372561.note: Karttunen's three conjectures, stated faithfully: A372555 = 7 on the 13th antidiagonal from 933 on, A372555 = 9 on the 30th from 58325 on, and A372555(A372560(n,k)) symmetric for n,k > 1. The grid construction reproduces A372560 (27,165,41,...; 233,933,... and 911,58325,...), and minCoins matches the least-Jacobsthal-count definition. An exact DP confirms the small entries (933 and 14933 give 7; 58325 and 933205 give 9; symmetric pairs agree). The 372-line proof uses base-4 digit-sum lower bounds and explicit representations. No prior proof was found. Second review: Faithful to Karttunen's three conjectures (it correctly targets the global-minimum count). The proof certifies minimum counts by base-4 digit-sum lower bounds attained by shifted representations, a genuine structural argument, not a finite check.

oeis-a221574.note: Barker's g.f. and order-4 recurrence (stated for n>=5, where all indices are terms) follow from the cubic a(n)=n^3-n^2+3n-1, which the proof derives by direct counting. The definition matches the entry's array condition, and no prior proof was found. Second review: Faithful (the n>=5 range for the recurrence is the correct reading) and true. It is an elementary count giving a cubic polynomial, hence routine.

OeisA179524.conjecture1.note: The statement matches Sun's 2010 conjecture exactly (p prime, p = 1 or 9 mod 20, p = x^2+5y^2, sum_{k<p} a(k) = 4x^2-2p mod p^2). RefactorableNumber.infinitely_many_conse.note: The formal-conjectures statement is Colton's 1999 Conjecture 2 (infinitely many n with n and n+1 refactorable, i.e. d(n) | n and d(n+1) | n+1), and it is faithful. Wikipedia and A036898 still list it as open, and searches of arXiv, Palomar and the web found no earlier proof. The 15 KB proof is a CRT-plus-sieve construction: it forces n = 3^a u and n+1 = 2^(e+2) v-type factorizations, then counts residue classes so that the remaining cofactors have controlled divisor counts. Prime-power divisor-count lemmas follow a sibling site proof (Zelinsky's progression conjecture). Substantive. Second review: Faithful statement of a 1999 conjecture listed as unsolved, with no prior proof found. The proof is a short (336-line) elementary sieve construction. That is surprising for a conjecture open since 1999, but it is kernel-checked against the upstream statement, so worth a human read before announcing.

oeis-a286051.note: Kimberling's conjecture 2n - a(n) in {0,1} is faithful. oeis-a285276.note: Kimberling's conjecture -2 < n*sqrt(2) - a(n) < 1 is faithful. The 0-limiting word is taken from the even iterates as A285274 describes, and it reproduces the 10^4-term b-file. oeis-a394666.note: The conjecture is stated for n >= 2. At n=1 the literal comment fails (a(1)=0 although n>5 is false), and the entry's own cross-reference treats n=1 as a zero, so the exclusion is a correct reading, not a weakening that the proof exploits. The proof is elementary: a prime 2n-1 > n does not divide n!, and for composite 2n-1 = d*e, d*e | n! (d=e handled via 2d <= n). Checked to n=3000. Second review: Elementary factorial-divisibility fact; no earlier written proof of this exact entry found, and the OEIS still calls it a conjecture. The n=1 exclusion is justified and matches the cross-reference. Routine.

oeis-a217214.note: Mathar's 2020 conjectured D-finite recurrence is stated with the g.f. defined implicitly by S^2 = 1-4x, S(0) = 1, and the coefficients expanded correctly. Since a 'D-finite with recurrence' claim is about eventual validity, restricting to n >= 5 is faithful. I recomputed the series: the left side is 3592 and 33072 at n = 3 and 4 (the docstring says so) and 0 for n = 5..38. A routine holonomic identity. Second review: True for n>=5, which is the usual 'valid for large n' reading of an OEIS D-finite recurrence. Routine. An announcement should mention that the recurrence fails at n=3,4 with the entry's initial terms.

oeis-a127752.note: The conjecture (a(n) mod 2 = A035263(n+1), with the offset shift the entry warns about) is stated faithfully. The truncated triangle 1/(3n+1)[k <= n <= 2k] reproduces the data (I inverted it for n < 34), and A035263 is encoded as the parity of v2(2n). The proof is short: it guesses the row sums u from the recursion u(2k) = 3 and u(2k+1) = 3 + u(k), checks A*u = 1, and reads off the parity. Only Karttunen's check to 2048 existed before. Routine. Second review: Faithful and true; a short elementary recursion for the inverse row sums gives the parity claim. Routine.

oeis-a172063.note: Mathar's 2016 recurrence 2n(n+6)(n+3)a(n) - (7n^3+59n^2+166n+160)a(n-1) - 2(2n+5)(n+4)(n+2)a(n-2) = 0 is stated for n >= 2, with the g.f. pinned down implicitly via S^2 = 1-4x, S(0) = 1, 2xc = 1-S, G(3S-1+4x) = 2c^6. The coefficients are expanded correctly. I recomputed the series and the recurrence vanishes for n = 2..39. It is still labelled a conjecture and is not in the Ekhad-Yang list of proved Mathar recurrences. A routine algebraic-g.f. identity. Second review: Faithful and true; a routine D-finite recurrence.

oeis-a007097.note: Ordowski's 2015 conjecture prod_{i<=n} log a(i) ~ a(n) is stated faithfully, with a(0) = 1 and a(n+1) = prime(a(n)). The disproof shows R(n) = prod log a(i)/a(n) cannot tend to 1. Each step multiplies R by at least 1 + 1/(16 log a(n+1)), via a second-order lower bound on pi(x), and these factors diverge like log log log a(n). Numerically R(n) climbs slowly (0.33, 0.57, 0.75, 0.85 at n = 5, 9, 13, 17), so the failure is not visible in the data. The effective PNT is reused, with credit, from an earlier site PR and Arithmetica4 (machinery only). I found no earlier refutation. Second review: A correct disproof of a conjecture that looks true numerically, because the divergence is extremely slow. It uses an effective PNT adapted, with credit, from Arithmetica4 and PR 5370. Genuine and non-routine.

oeis-a158197.note: The first of Mathar's two 2015 recurrences, 4(n+1)a(n) + (23-81n)a(n-1) + 10(51n-70)a(n-2) + 500(5-2n)a(n-3) = 0, is stated for n >= 3. G is pinned down by G(1-4xc^2) = 1 - x^2c^4 with c the Catalan series. I recomputed the series (1, 4, 23, 140, 866, ...) and the recurrence vanishes for n = 3..39. The second, order-2 conjecture in the entry is not formalized, which is fine. Routine. Second review: Faithful to the first of two Mathar recurrences, and true; routine.

oeis-a286014.note: The conjecture (A286014 = row sums of A211343) is stated faithfully, with A211343 from its name (column k is 1, 2, 3, ... interleaved with k-1 zeros, starting at row k(k+1)/2). I checked the identity for n < 200. Trivial: n has a partition into k consecutive parts iff k | n - k(k+1)/2, and its smallest part is then (n - k(k+1)/2)/k + 1, which is exactly the column entry. Second review: Faithful and true. It follows immediately by matching each k-part consecutive partition with column k of A211343; routine.

oeis-a278405.note: Sun's 2016 conjecture (for primes p > 5 and n >= 1, (a(pn) - a(n))/(pn)^3 is a p-adic integer) is stated faithfully: the quotient is formed in Q and p must not divide its reduced denominator. The entry records only Sun's proof of the weaker p^3 n^2 version, and I found no later proof. I checked the claim for p = 7, 11, 13 and n <= 8. The 1270-line proof uses q-Lucas and Gaussian-coefficient lemmas credited to an earlier site PR (A179524 conjecture 4; machinery only). Sibling Sun conjectures A275027 and A278415 were solved on the site the same day with the same toolkit, but they are different sequences. Substantive. Second review: Faithful statement of a Sun conjecture with no recorded proof. The 1272-line proof (q-binomial/Gaussian-coefficient lemmas credited to @TaifengYi from the A179524 conj.4 work) appears to be a genuine new supercongruence; not routine.

oeis-a140829.note: Barker's 2019 recurrence a(n) = -a(n-1)+a(n-2)+a(n-3)+a(n-4)+a(n-5) for n > 12 is stated faithfully, with a(n) = ceil(F(n)/a(n-1)) over Q, and I checked it up to n = 80. The proof establishes the closed forms a(2k+4) = L(k+1)+1 and a(2k+5) = F(k+4)-1 by joint induction with Fibonacci/Lucas identities. Nye's 2026 line in the entry states the odd-index half without proof. Routine. Second review: Faithful and true. The proof needs closed forms for both parities of a ceiling recursion, proved by Fibonacci-identity induction. It is a recurrence identity, so routine, though not a one-liner.

oeis-a244713.note: x^2+xy-2y^2 = (x-y)(x+2y) has discriminant 9, and the primitively represented numbers repeat with 11 terms in every block of 27 (checked against the data: a(n+11)-a(n)=27). Barker's recurrence a(n)=a(n-1)+a(n-11)-a(n-12) for n>12 follows. Routine. Second review: True and faithful; follows from an elementary periodic characterization of primitive representations by a split form. Routine.

oeis-a083020.note: The conjecture (every 3^(3^n)+2 is squarefree, offset 0) is stated verbatim. The disproof shows 29^2 | 3^(3^73)+2 via 3^73 = 31 mod 812 = phi(841). I checked that pow(3, 3^73, 841) = 839, and n = 73 is the least such n with p = 29. I found no earlier record of this counterexample in the entry or the libraries searched. It is a finite search for a square factor in an exponential tower, so routine. Second review: Correct disproof: 29^2 | 3^(3^73)+2. A smaller counterexample exists, n=18 with 31^2 (worth mentioning when announcing). Routine finite check.

oeis-a288932.note: Kimberling's conjecture (the n-th iterate, counting 00 as the first, has A123720(n) = 2^n + 2^(n-1) - n letters) is stated faithfully. The step function reproduces Mathematica's left-to-right, non-overlapping StringReplace, which I re-simulated: the length formula holds for n = 1..19 and the iterates match the listed ones. The proof is a block decomposition (10 -> 10 10 1, 1 -> 1, 00 -> 10 00), so routine. Second review: True and faithful. Routine word-combinatorics induction.

oeis-a002107.note: Kotesovec's Sep 2026 conjecture is stated faithfully: sum |a(k)| ~ sqrt(8 pi log(2+sqrt3)/3) n/sqrt(log n) and sum a(k)^2 ~ log(7+4 sqrt3) n, with a(n) the n-th coefficient of prod(1-x^k)^2 (both constants agree numerically with his 3.32158..., 2.63391...). The orders of growth were known, and Finch (2007) gives the constants as Euler products via Selberg-Delange. But the entry still labels these closed forms a conjecture, and I found no earlier proof of them. The 270 KB proof rebuilds the asymptotics, with Gaussian-integer and PNT-in-progressions machinery credited to other site PRs (lemmas only, not this problem). Substantive. Second review: True and faithful. The asymptotic shapes were already known (Finch 2007); the new content is identifying Finch's Euler products with L(1,chi) values for characters mod 12 (log(2+sqrt3) etc.), which is a routine class-number-formula evaluation, though the Lean proof re-derives the full asymptotics. Proof reuses many internal site libraries (credited).

mo-191547.note: Newman's question (is {floor(n^(3/2))} a basis of order 3?) is stated as: every m is val(a)+val(b)+val(c) with val(n) = Nat.sqrt(n^3) = floor(n^(3/2)). oeis-a138904.note: Statement faithful to the first conjecture: among binary expansions of length n, the attained numbers of rotational symmetries are exactly the divisors of n. oeis-a145052.note: Faithful: for n >= 3 every cell lies in some 3x3 block, so the nonnegative entries are forced into {0,1} and Fin 2 loses nothing; a(n) = 0 for n < 3 matches the g.f. oeis-a156201.note: Faithful: the numerator of E_n(1/8) equals 8^n E_n(1/8) (checked for n < 25), and Gladkovskii's continued fraction is encoded by depth-N convergents with tail 1, claimed for n <= 2N. The proof derives exact tails via Laplace transforms of e^(-3t) sinh^k sech^(k+1)(4t), a classical Rogers/Stieltjes-type argument. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and true. It reduces by a binomial (Euler) transform to Stieltjes' classical continued fraction for the secant numbers, so routine; the proof is long only because of Lean series plumbing.

OeisA79727.conjecture1.note: Bala's conjecture 1 (2024): for p in A003625 (p = 3,5,6 mod 7), a(p^2) = 8 + p^2 mod p^3. The formal statement matches the entry word for word, and I checked it numerically for p = 3, 5, 13, 17, 19. The proof extends the site's earlier conjecture-2 proof (PR 6898) with Lucas vanishing and C(2p^2,p^2)^3 = 8 mod p^3, using CM/Picard-Fuchs arguments. Epoch's runs on the sibling conjecture 2 all failed. I found nothing on Palomar, in Fried's four OEIS papers or in Z.-H. Sun's 2026 preprint arXiv:2611.16834. Second review: Faithful, open, and new as far as every tracker I could reach shows. The proof (230 KB) also proves conjecture 2 on the way. I did not audit the Lean itself.

arxiv-1912.11230.note: Best-Wanless Conjecture 31: t_ac + t_bc + t_ad + t_bd = 0 mod 4 for every Latin square. The statement matches the source, including its definition of transversals of the (n-1)x(n-1) Latin array (min(m,n) entries, no shared row, column or symbol) and all a, b, c, d, not necessarily distinct. Brute force over all Latin squares of order <= 4 and 300 of order 5 found no violation. The proof is a genuine algebraic argument using signed sums of products prod_s(z + c_s(U,T)). I found no prior proof on the web, Palomar or openai/math. Second review: A real 2019 conjecture, now proved by a parity/sign argument (66 KB Lean). I found no prior proof.

arxiv-2008.10398.note: Fink's Conjecture 1: for every k there are ample numbers (a(n) > n, where a is the recursive divisor count of Definition 1) not divisible by the first k primes. The Lean recursiveDivisors matches Definition 1 (a(10)=6, a(12)=16, a(216)=504 checked), and 'p <= k' is an equivalent way of excluding the first primes. The proof is an elementary mass argument using divergence of sum 1/p over primes > k. The source and later Fink versions list it as open, and I found no prior proof. Second review: Short and elegant, a Hille-style argument. It is new as far as I can find, though an expert might call it folklore-level.

arxiv-2101.07103.note: Counterexample to Estrada-Mugnolo Conjecture 4.13 (v2): two K4's joined through a path 0-4-5 on 9 vertices. I recomputed it in floating point: the hubs-attracting index is about 68.1, above the ordinary index 61. That violates R_0 >= R_{-1} under both the Moore-Penrose inverse (the formal choice) and the paper's V Lambda^+ V^{-1} spectral inverse, so the disproof does not depend on that modelling choice. The conjecture does hold on all connected graphs up to 6 vertices (consistent with the authors' search up to 8). The proof is a finite rational certificate, and I found no prior counterexample. Second review: The counterexample refutes Conjecture 4.13 under both readings of the hubs-biased resistance. The formal statement follows the paper's literal 'Moore-Penrose' wording, which is evidently not what the authors computed. The write-up should mention that, and should say that the same graph also breaks the spectral version.

arxiv-2510.24280.note: Counterexample to Conjecture 4 (FvF never worse than AvA for either player): S = {3,5,12,16,30}, heap 83 gives FvF (48,35) and AvA (47,36), which I recomputed independently. The Lean recurrence matches Definition 2 of the paper, with friendly maximizing and antagonistic minimizing the opponent's total over the tied moves. The authors only tested max S <= 25, which explains why they missed it (here max S = 30). The latest version (v2, Jan 2026) still states the conjecture, and I found no prior counterexample. Second review: A clean finite counterexample to a 2025 conjecture, verified by kernel evaluation and by my own recomputation.

mo-267889.note: The asker's proposed identity E|B\A| = E|B|(1 - E|A|/n) fails at n = m = 2. By hand: E|A| = 3/2, E|B| = 5/4 and E|B\A| = 1/4, while the right side is 5/16. The formal model (second sample of size |A| drawn conditionally uniformly) matches the question. The question has no answers or comments, so this is an elementary but unrecorded refutation. Second review: A correct refutation by the smallest case. It is trivial, but the question really was unanswered.

mo-298064.note: The inequality |S_0(t,m)| >= |S_a(t,m)| is refuted. The Lean witness is the degenerate m = t = 1 case over F_2 ([1] has trace 1 and no rank-1 1x1 matrix has trace 0). My enumeration shows the claim also fails in non-degenerate cases: F_2 with m = 2, t = 1 (1 vs 2), F_3 with m = 3, t = 1 (8 vs 9), and F_5 with m = 2, t = 2 (16 vs 21). So the refutation is genuine, not an edge-case exploit. The question has no answers. Second review: Correct disproof. For an announcement, a nondegenerate counterexample (e.g. q=3, m=4, t=3) should go next to the 1x1 one.

mo-313415.note: Affirmative answer: with f(n) = (n+1)^3 ceil((32/27)^{n/3+1}), m = 1/2 beats every other m in [0,1], for any coupling of the arrays. The statement asks for this for every joint distribution satisfying row-wise independence and the Bin(n,1/2) law, which is stronger than any reading of the question. The proof uses threshold 2^{n/3} with binomial and first-moment bounds, a real argument. The question has no answers, and I found no prior solution. Second review: A substantive affirmative answer (m=1/2 with exponentially many agents), formalized with explicit bounds. I did not audit the 50 KB Lean, but the mathematics is consistent.

mo-331165.note: Berger's conjecture (div(rho B x v) = 0 for all B forces v parallel to grad rho) is refuted with constant rho and constant v. That witness is degenerate, but the conjecture also fails for non-constant rho: the condition is v x grad rho = rho curl v, and v = grad(psi)/rho solves it for every psi. The formal statement (all nonzero B, positive differentiable rho, differentiable v) matches the question, and it has no answers. Second review: The refutation is correct, but the Lean counterexample uses constant rho, which the asker probably did not intend. The announcement should give the general solution v=grad(phi)/rho (e.g. rho=e^x, v=e^{-x} e_y) so it cannot be dismissed as an edge case.

mo-479805.note: Proof of Kiwi's binomial-cdf inequality (1): (F(k)+F(k+1))/((n-k)(F(k-1)+F(k))) is nonincreasing in n. The formal statement matches the question: 0 < p < 1, m < n, 1 <= k <= m-1, and the same grouping. I verified it in exact rational arithmetic for 2275 cases (n <= 15, five values of p) with no violations. The proof uses a beta-integral representation, integration by parts and moment positivity. The question has no answers, and I found nothing on Palomar. Second review: A genuine proof of an inequality that was unanswered on MO.

mo-513259.note: Both of joro's 2026 conjectures are proved: per(M^{-1}) = 1 mod 8 and 2 per(M) + per(M^{-1}) = 3 mod 24, for adjacency matrices invertible mod 8 or 24, with the inverse taken in ZMod, which is equivalent to reducing the rational inverse. I checked every graph on n <= 6 vertices (13917 and 12401 cases) with no failures. The proof (Ryser expansion over Boolean faces mod 8, a mixed-moment identity over F_3) is genuine. The question has no answers, and I found nothing on Palomar. Second review: A recent (July 2026) MO conjecture, proved in 63 KB of Lean. Nothing prior found.

oeis-a000247.note: L. Edson Jeffery's (2012) conjectured matrix identity: for n > 2, entry v_{n-2} of A^n * 1, with A the n x n tridiagonal unit-primitive matrix whose last diagonal entry is 1, equals 2^n - n - 2. The zero-based index n-3 is correct, and I checked numerically for n = 3..19. The proof is a short dynamic-programming induction on the top diagonals. The entry still labels the identity a conjecture, and I found no prior proof. Second review: Correct and faithful. A short dynamic-programming identity.

oeis-a002857.note: Mathar's 2022 conjecture A002857(n) = A055621(n) - A055152(n), proved by the bijection between Boolean functions with f(0)=0, f(1)=1 and families of nonempty subsets containing the full set, equivariant under S_n. The Lean definitions reproduce the OEIS data (1,3,20,996 for Post functions; 1,4,34,1952 for covers; 0,1,14,956 for proper covers; brute force n <= 4). Elementary, and I found no prior proof. Second review: True by a one-line bijection; routine.

oeis-a007062.note: Kurkov's conjecture A007062(n) = A057030(n-1) + 1 (n >= 2). The Lean P(n) block-reversal maps for both entries reproduce the OEIS data (first 24 terms of each, checked). The proof observes that on positions >= 2 the A007062 map is the A057030 map shifted by one, and inducts. Short and elementary; no prior proof found (both entries still say 'Conjecture'). Second review: Correct and routine. It also settles the site's open oeis-a057030, which should be linked or closed as a duplicate.

oeis-a013302.note: Both of Mathar's 2014 recurrences for A013302, with the sequence defined from Jovovic's e.g.f. (2-x^2)/(2 sqrt(1-x^2)). oeis-a093210.note: Stephan's conjecture a(n) = A060477(n+4) - 2 is stated faithfully: T(n,k) = A051168(n+4,k+2), k=0..n, matches the Mathematica program of A092964 (k+1 for k=1..n+1) and the data rows 1; 2,2; 2,3,2. oeis-a093726.note: He's 2026 conjecture Im c(n) = A317974(n+1)/A138573(n) is stated faithfully for all representations c(n) = (x+yi)/d, with the convergent recursion matching the entry's examples (c(3) = (8+4i)/5 gives 4/5 = A317974(4)/A138573(3)). oeis-a097180.note: Mathar's order-3 recurrence is stated faithfully for n >= 3; I checked symbolically that the expanded coefficients equal Mathar's factored ones and that the recurrence holds for the series of 2/((1-8x)+(1-8x)^(3/4)) up to n=40. oeis-a100833.note: Israel's 2019 conjectured formula (1 if n=1 mod 3, 2 if n=2 mod 3, else 3+v2(n/3)) is stated for all n>=1 against a faithful greedy definition (least positive letter avoiding a palindromic suffix of length >=2 and a square suffix). I recomputed the greedy word by brute force to n=1500 and it matches. The proof is a genuine combinatorics-on-words argument (no palindromes, no squares via a ruler lemma, minimality). No prior proof found; note the statement credits @frido22 while the PR is by Salofe. Second review: Correct; a short combinatorics-on-words argument.

oeis-a102319.note: Both of Mathar's recurrences (order 6 for n>=6, order 4 for n>=4) are stated with coefficients copied correctly and a(n) = sum C(n,k)C(2k,k)(1+(-1)^(n-k))/2 as in the entry; both hold for n<80. Proof derives three-term recurrences for the two binomial transforms and combines them; routine holonomic work. No prior proof found. Second review: Routine.

oeis-a102880.note: Mathar's recurrence is stated with the entry's g.f. ((1-x^2)/(1+x^2))c(x/(1+x^2)) as definition. It fails at n=4 (left side 3), so the statement starts at n=5; the entry gives no range, and from n=5 on the identity holds (checked to n=40), which is the usual reading for such g.f.-derived recurrences. The restriction is disclosed and reasonable. Routine D-finite derivation; no prior proof found. Second review: Routine. Mathar's recurrence holds exactly from n=5. Say 'for n>=5' explicitly in any announcement.

oeis-a106249.note: Barry's conjecture a(n) = Sum_{k<=n} Jacobi(2^k, 2k+1) is stated faithfully for all n>=0 with the entry's g.f. as definition. Since (2^k|2k+1) = chi_8(2k+1)^k is 4-periodic (-1 iff k=1 mod 4), the claim is elementary; checked to n=200. thatnealpatel/proofs has an A106249 file, but it refutes Lagneau's different left-half-plane conjecture, so it is not a prior proof of this one. Second review: Routine periodicity argument.

oeis-a106391.note: Both Mathar recurrences (order 6 for n>=6, order 4 for n>=4) are transcribed correctly with a(n) = Sum binomial(n,2k) binomial(2(n-2k), n-2k+1) from the entry; both hold for n<80. Routine holonomic proof via the binomial and inverse binomial transforms of binomial(2j,j+1). No prior proof found; the statement credits @JeremyDevs while the PR is by Salofe. Second review: Routine.

oeis-a107793.note: Disproof of Sloane's 2018 conjecture that A107793, relabeled (5->6, 4->5) and with the first two terms dropped, is a shift of A275925. The definitions (f-morphism limit S[3k+1], sigma-trajectory of 3) are faithful and reproduce both entries' data, and the statement allows shifts in both directions. Numerically the best shift (11) agrees only for 41 terms. In ~10^5-term windows no shift in [-20000,20000] even agrees eventually. The proof writes the relabeled word as a sigma-image and uses aperiodicity of A275925; no prior refutation found. Second review: Sloane's 2018 'appears to be a shifted version' is false: the two words share a language but are not shifts of each other. The disproof is genuinely new.

oeis-a108600.note: Mathar's order-6 recurrence for n>=6 is transcribed correctly; the normalised g.f. used as the definition equals the entry's (Vatter) g.f. as a series (checked to x^40), and the recurrence holds for n<40. It is about the g.f., not the pattern class. Routine certificate proof from S^2 = 1-4x; no prior proof found. The statement credits @vivanpoddar, the proof and PR credit ivillar. Second review: Routine.

oeis-a110521.note: Mathar's order-5 recurrence for n>=5 is transcribed correctly, with the entry's g.f. 1/(1-(x+x^2)c(3x)) as the definition (6xc = 1-S, S^2 = 1-12x); it holds for n<40. Routine D-finite derivation; no prior proof found. Second review: Routine.

oeis-a112000.note: Mathar's first-order recurrence n(4n+5)a(n) + (2n+3)(n+2)(4n+9)a(n-1) = 0 is stated faithfully for n>=1, with a(n) = A111999(n+3,2)/2 and A111999 given by its formula-section recurrence (it reproduces rows -1; 3,2; -15,-20,-6). Checked for n<40. The proof finds closed forms for columns 0-2 by induction; routine. Second review: Routine closed form.

oeis-a116637.note: Mathar's recurrence is stated for n>=3, with the entry's explicit factorial formula (a(2k+1)=2*A006013(k), a(2k+2)=2*A001764(k+1), a(0)=1) as the definition; it reproduces the data. oeis-a119012.note: Mathar's recurrence for n>=3 (offset 1) is stated with correctly expanded coefficients, and a(n) = [x^n] of Deutsch's g.f. oeis-a119936.note: Lang's conjectured a(n)/n^3 = A002944(n)^2 is formalized as lcm_j den(M^3(n,j)) = n*lcm(1..n)^2, with M^3(n,j) = (1/n) Sum_{i=j..n} (1/i) Sum_{k=j..i} 1/k, which matches the cube of the mean matrix. I checked it exactly for n <= 150; it reproduces the data 1,8,108,576,18000,... The proof needs an exact p-adic valuation argument (a lower bound from a column j = p^e). No prior proof found; Meijer's formula in A027451 is a related unproved statement. Second review: Correct and apparently new as a proof. The announcement should note Meijer's 2009 unproved formula in A027451.

oeis-a121580.note: Mathar's recurrence for n>=5 is stated faithfully. The definition is Deutsch's first-order recurrence a(n) = a(n-1) + (n-1)!(1+n(n-1)/2) from the entry, which reproduces the data. The proof is a linear combination of four instances of that recurrence, which is routine; I checked it for n<30. No prior proof found. Second review: Routine consequence of a formula already in the entry.

oeis-a062091.note: Mathar's 2025 conjecture a(n) = 2*A062090(n-1) for n >= 3 is stated faithfully, with both greedy sequences built over running products (least positive even / odd non-divisor). The definitions reproduce both data lines, and the identity holds for n <= 40. It is essentially immediate from the two entries' (unproved, Munn-corrected) characterizations {2,4} U 2{p^(2^k)} and {1} U {p^(2^k)}, which the proof re-derives. Routine. Second review: Faithful and true; Mathar's identity is immediate from the Fermi-Dirac-type characterizations recorded in both entries. Routine.

oeis-a064873.note: He's 2025 conjecture a(n) = A064874(n - A064874(n)^2) is stated faithfully. a and A064874 are the nested Nat.find minima of the lexicographically least 4-square decomposition, offset 0, and the definition reproduces the data. I checked it for n <= 3000. The proof is a short minimality argument: n - b^2 = a^2+c^2+d^2 has first part 0, and a smaller second part would give a smaller first part for n. True but elementary. Second review: Faithful and true. He's conjecture is a definitional consequence of lexicographic minimality (proof is ~15 lines, no number theory). Routine; it is an easy problem rather than a formalization artifact.

oeis-a067016.note: Barker's closed form 2a(n) = -3 + (-1)^n + 4n for n >= 4 and his g.f. are stated faithfully. a(0..3) = 1,4,3,2, and a(n+1) = max over 0 <= i <= n of a(i)+a(n-i) for n >= 3, as in the name. The definition reproduces the data, and the closed form holds for n < 200. Routine strong induction on the max-plus recurrence; the entry already notes that the first differences are ultimately periodic. Second review: Faithful and true; Barker's closed form and g.f. Routine.

oeis-a073409.note: Ordowski's characterization (a(n) is the largest prime r <= 2n+1 with r*num(B_2n) == -den(B_2n) mod r^2) is stated faithfully over Mathlib's bernoulli. I checked it exactly for n <= 40. It is a short corollary of von Staudt-Clausen (in Mathlib): the primes satisfying the congruence are exactly those with (r-1) | 2n, and the den is their product. Routine. Second review: Faithful and true; Ordowski's characterization is a direct restatement of von Staudt-Clausen. Routine.

oeis-a074358.note: Wu's g.f., Barker's Binet closed form (n > 0) and order-4 recurrence (n > 4) are stated faithfully for the q^1 coefficient of nu(n) with (b, lambda) = (2,2). nu reproduces the example polynomials and the data. Second review: Faithful and true; rational g.f. for a low q-coefficient of a q-recurrence. Routine.

RudinsConjecture.rudins_conjecture_uniqu.reason: The formal 'uniqueness' says that for all N>=6 every non-trivial progression attaining Qmax(N) has difference exactly 24. At N=6 the progression 120n+49 (49, 169, 289, 529) attains Q(6)=4, which refutes that claim trivially. The literature 'super-strong' conjecture of González-Jiménez–Xarles asserts uniqueness only up to equivalence and only for N = GP_k + 1 >= 8, so the formalization (all N>=6, literal q=24) is stronger than the real conjecture. The disproof exploits this mismatch and says nothing about the actual conjecture.

Bugeaud06.problem_10_6_variant_1.reason: The proof is a genuine, elementary construction: m enumerates {a*2^t : 1 <= a <= floor(log t)+1}. Density for every irrational xi follows from Dirichlet's theorem plus doubling, and consecutive ratios are >= 1 + (1/2)/log n. But Bugeaud's Problem 10.6 ('find a very rapidly increasing sequence...') is open-ended and not a precise statement. 'IsGenuinelySublacunary' (ratio floor 1 + c/log n, i.e. growth only about exp(cn/log n)) is a threshold the formalizers chose themselves, and the same argument works with any unbounded multiplier bound A(t). So it is not what Bugeaud asks, and proving it does not solve Problem 10.6. At most it settles a weak, catalogue-invented variant.

Green44.green_44.reason: The disproof only works because the formalization quantifies over all N, with no 'N sufficiently large' condition. It takes N = 100000 and the 1000 primes in [20011, 30161], which are < N^{9/10} = 31622 only because N^{1/10} < 10. Each A_i is the block of residues 10002..10001 + floor(p_i/2), so all of [1, 10001] survives and 10*|remaining| = 100010 > N. For large N (any N > 10^10) every prime is below N/10, and this trivial block trick is impossible. Green's question (from Erdős, contrasting with the large-sieve range p < N^{1/2}) is about the asymptotic regime, so nothing was learned about the real problem.

Erdos354.erdos_354.parts.ii.reason: The formal statement reads 'what if 2 is replaced by some gamma in (1,2)' as an EXISTENTIAL over gamma. The proof (a port of Kenta Kitamura's development) just picks gamma = sqrt(golden ratio) and shows that a SINGLE floor sequence floor(gamma^n alpha) is complete for every alpha>0. The second sequence and the hypothesis that alpha/beta is irrational are never used, which shows the formalization has removed the actual content of the question (whether, or for which, gamma in (1,2) the two-sequence statement holds as it does for gamma=2). This does not answer the question as erdosproblems.com poses it.

mo-93022.reason: The formal statement takes literally the question's 'that is' clause: v is connecting if for all p != q some k > 0 gives p.v^k = q or q.v^k = p. It then asks for such a v of length <= n-1 whenever one exists. The disproof is a 5-state, 3-letter automaton with a reset letter, checked by decide. It has a connecting word of length 6, and every word of length <= 4 is constant or preserves a nontrivial 2-colouring. Under that literal reading the counterexample is valid. However, the question is not precise or self-consistent. It asks about words whose 'underlying graph is connected' (Berlinkov's one-cluster setting), and in the comments the author says one may also assume that w takes A into one state. A constant map is never connecting in the literal sense once n >= 3, so the literal clause cannot be what was meant. A commenter also notes that assumptions are missing, which makes the answer obviously 'no'. Under the graph-connectivity reading the counterexample fails: its length-1 reset letter has a connected (one-cluster) functional graph. So the disproof settles a literal reading the author's own clarifications contradict, not a precise open question.

Erdos40.erdos_40.reason: The upstream erdos_40 is a 'question value' statement: {g | g -> infinity and Erdos40For g} = erdos_40.answer, where answer is a sorry placeholder. The PR proves only that this holds if answer is replaced by its own OMA.answer. OMA.answer is {g | g -> infinity and for all k there is T >= k such that every p in maximalProfiles k T violates a finite inequality against sqrt(i)/g(i)}. The proof gets there by rewriting with erdos40For_iff_finite (a compactness truncation to finite sets with representation count <= k) and finite_iff_profile_obstruction. So the 'answer' is a mechanical restatement of the defining predicate Erdos40For through finite truncations, not an explicit characterisation of the admissible g. The file header admits that the criterion 'does not settle whether there is any divergent denominator satisfying it', so it does not even settle the weaker variant or Erdős #28. The extra side results (log-band and fourth-root counterexamples) are partial and are not the stated problem. erdosproblems.com still lists #40 as open with 0 proof claims; this is a trivialised answer, not a solution.

mo-407245.reason: The MO question asks for the smallest l (as a function of k,n, or even an asymptotic bound) such that any l equipartitions of a kn-set force a pair to share a block in at least half of them. The formal statement does not give an answer: it defines threshold k n through hasOrthogonal k n 3 and hasOrthogonal k n 4, which are brute-force `decide` searches over every family of partitions, and only proves that the minimum is 3, 4 or nonexistent depending on those uncomputed predicates. The proof is the easy reduction: a pair that meets at most once can't reach r/2 for r=3,4, and repeating 4 pairwise orthogonal equipartitions cyclically defeats every r >= 3. Peter Taylor's comment under the question already gives this repetition idea (using Kirkman's 7 orthogonal partitions). The real content, namely for which (k,n) 3 or 4 mutually orthogonal equipartitions exist (for k=n this is the existence of 1 or 2 MOLS of order n, so e.g. k=n=6 gives 4), is left undetermined. The theorem therefore restates the question in terms of an unsolved design-existence predicate rather than settling it.

mo-148821.reason: The MathOverflow question (no answers, no comments) is open-ended: 'what can we say about |M_1 ∪ ... ∪ M_b| compared to a maximum b-matching, is anything known about the ratio?'. It gives no precise conjecture or candidate value, and the statement file says so itself. The formal 'answer' does not compute the ratio. It proves that p/q is guaranteed iff a finite integer certificate exists (`certified b p q`: labels, weights and linear inequalities over subsets of Fin b). That is an LP-duality/blow-up characterisation, which in effect restates the question as a finite linear program. It gives no explicit bound, does not even recover the 1/2 the asker noted for b = 1, 2, and says nothing about how the ratio behaves as b grows. The Lean proof (Farkas lemma plus a blow-up construction realising the dual) is a real argument, and legalRounds does faithfully encode successive maximal matchings. But it does not settle the source question, which is not a precise yes/no problem.

oeis-a346214.reason: The disproof attacks only the second conjunct, the finite formula T(n,n-j) = A002884(n)/(A002884(j)·2^(n-(j-1)^2)), stated 'for j < 2n'. The range 'j < 2n' is plainly a typo by Critzer: it allows every j < n, and the formula already fails at n = 3, j = 2 (1 vs 14) and at n = 4, j = 2 (315 vs 420). It holds in the checked cases with 2j < n (n = 3, j = 1: 21; n = 4, j = 1: 1260; n = 5, j = 2: 104160), so the intended statement is evidently 'for n > 2j'. So the conjecture has not really been refuted.

Erdos691.erdos_691.note: Erdos asks for 'a necessary and sufficient condition' on A for M_A to have density 1, which is an open-ended request. The formal statement erdos_691.answer = (fun A => (multiples A).HasDensity 1) is satisfied by the tautological answer. So it accepts any equivalent predicate and cannot tell a real answer from a restatement. The submitted OMA.answer says that A meets every 'AdmissibleTest'. A test is an arbitrary infinite sequence of finite divisor-closed sets on prime blocks satisfying a harmonic-mass retention inequality, so the criterion quantifies over an uncountable family of obstruction certificates. It is a dual reformulation of the Behrend property, not an arithmetic condition on A. The forum thread notes that the analogous finite-approximation criterion is the classical Davenport-Erdos fact (Hall-Tenenbaum (1.3)) and does not count as a solution. The file says it is a port of github.com/Ghuffy1/erdos691, and erdosproblems.com/691 remains open. The proof is valid but does not solve the problem as posed.

Erdos357.erdos_357.parts.ii.bigO_version.note: The question is 'how does f(n) grow / find a good explicit g with f = O(g)'. The real open problem is whether f(n) = o(n). The formal statement f =O[atTop] answer is trivially satisfied by answer(n) = n, since a strictly increasing sequence in [1,n] has at most n terms. So it is vacuous. The submitted answer (44273/90000)n + 2 sqrt n + 177792 is again linear, so the Big-O conclusion carries no information beyond the trivial bound; the sharper constant (about 0.4919 < 1/2, said to be from Chandler Snively's 2026 preprint) is invisible to the statement. Known upper bounds on the page and forum are (2/3 - 1/512)n (Coppersmith-Phillips), about 0.8727n (Beker), and a claimed n/2 + O(n^{2/3}) (Lenthall-Cleary, July 2026). The PR itself concedes that 'whether f(n)=o(n) remains open'. Not a solution.

Erdos692.erdos_692.parts.ii.note: Erdos asks where, for fixed n, delta_1(n,m) attains its maximum. The formal statement only requires some function answer(n) at which the maximum over m > n+1 is attained. The submitted OMA.answer(n) is literally the argmax of the exact density, computed as residue counts mod m!, over the candidates m in [n+2, n+2+A+B], where A = (3^{2(n+1)^2})! and B is a factorial of a factorial. This is a brute-force argmax of the very quantity asked about, with a tower-type cutoff. It proves that the maximum exists and is attained below an astronomically large bound, but it gives no information about where the maximum lies, which is what Erdos asked; the PR concedes 'the cutoff is too large for practical computation'. erdosproblems.com/692 (Cambie: superpolynomially many local maxima) gives no closed form, and the question remains open.

Erdos732.erdos_732.parts.i.note: Erdos asks whether there are reasonable necessary and sufficient conditions for a sequence (X_i) to be block-compatible, i.e. realizable as the block sizes of a pairwise balanced design. The formal 'question value' statement accepts any predicate equivalent to membership in blockSizeProfiles n. The submitted OMA.answer says that s is sorted and that a coefficient of prod over all T subset of [n] with |T|>=2 of (1 + x^{term T}) is positive. By the proof's own lemma coeff_pos, that coefficient is positive iff there is a family of blocks covering every pair exactly once with the size multiset s. So it is the definition of block-compatibility re-encoded as a generating function, i.e. exhaustive search. The PR says 'this criterion makes no efficiency claim'. This is a restatement, not a solution.

Erdos1017.erdos_1017.upper_bound.note: Erdős asks to 'estimate' (sharpen) the clique-partition number f(n,k) for k > n^2/4. The formal 'upper_bound' only asks for some function with f(n,k) <= answer(n,k). Any known bound satisfies it: the API lemma f <= k, or Erdős–Goodman–Pósa's n^2/4. The supplied OMA.answer is min(n^2/4, k - C(r,2) + 1) with r = n - (C(n,2)-k). That is EGP plus the elementary bound 'a clique on n-q vertices, then the remaining edges one by one'. No matching lower bound and no asymptotic estimate is given. The one-sided statement is essentially vacuous as a formalization of the problem, so problem 1017 is not solved.

Erdos422.erdos_422.variants.growth_rate.note: 'How does f grow?' for Hofstadter's Q-sequence is formalized only as a one-sided bound f =O(answer), with answer supplied by the solver. OMA.answer = n, and the proof is f(n) <= n, which is built into the IsHofstadterQ predicate itself (it requires f(n-1) < n so that the recurrence is defined). The file also proves f(n) > c n infinitely often for c < 1/2, but the solution does not use it, and neither describes the actual growth (conjecturally f(n) ≈ n/2 with chaotic fluctuations). It is not even known that f is defined for all n. The answer is the trivial bound, so nothing about problem 422 is settled.

Erdos450.erdos_450.note: Erdős asks how large y(eps,n) must be, i.e. for an estimate of the threshold's size; the page discusses regimes such as y ~ 2n for eps << 1/n and no finite y at all for larger eps. The formal statement asks for exact equality windowThreshold eps n = answer eps n with an unconstrained answer function. The proof's OMA.answer is just a finite sup over residues x, r modulo P = lcm(n+1,...,2n-1) of a 'cutoff' solving the periodic counting inequality, i.e. the definition of the threshold re-expressed as a brute-force computation over one period. This proves only that the threshold is computable from periodicity and says nothing about how y(eps,n) grows in eps and n. The formalisation admits this tautological answer, so the open problem is not solved.

arxiv-2205.09212.reason: The source ('Primal Conjecture', §11 of Marrero–Acuña) is the vague implication 'phi_a op phi_b == phi_c (mod 9) => exists Z_a, Z_b with Z_a op Z_b = Z_c'. The paper then asks whether all members of the class are solutions or only some, and writes '... => ¬∀ Z_a, Z_b / Z_a op Z_b = Z_c'. The formal statement fixes the strongest reading: every z in column c is exactly x op y for some x, y in columns a, b. The disproof (5+6 -> 2, z=2) exploits a small-number edge case of exactly that reading. The paper itself signals the ∀ version need not hold, and the natural ∃ reading is trivially true. The source is not a well-posed problem, and the 'disproof' does not refute anything the authors claim.

It is a valid answer to an idle OEIS question, not a new theorem.

The [1,n] version follows by compactness. The infinite Hindman version was answered negatively by Deuber-Gunderson-Hindman-Strauss (1997). The erdosproblems.com remark that this 'remains open' appears to be out of date.

mo-341315.reason: The formal statement is the asker's Question 1 with his clarification k >= 2: there are infinitely many primes p with some k >= 2 and 1 <= n < p such that p^k > n*rad(p^(k+1)-n). The proof takes n = 1 and k = 2^p - 1. By Euler's theorem 2^(p+1) divides p^(2^p) - 1, so rad(p^(k+1)-1) <= 2(p^(k+1)-1)/2^(p+1) < p^k. With n = 1 the inequality says exactly that (1, p^(k+1)-1, p^(k+1)) is an abc-hit, c > rad(abc). The question is therefore an immediate instance of the classical construction of infinitely many abc-hits (a = 1, c a 2-power power of an odd number, with b divisible by a high power of 2; Wikipedia's abc conjecture article gives the 2^(6n) variant). It works for every odd prime. Greg Martin's comment already points out that the k = 1 case is easy. The proof is correct, but the question is answered by a standard textbook argument and was not a genuinely open problem.

oeis-a259661.reason: The formal statement is Colin Barker's empirical recurrence and generating function 1/((1-x)(1-10x)(1+x^2)) for the middle column of Rule 54 read in base 10. The cellular automaton definition matches the OEIS data, so the formalization is faithful. But the whole Rule 54 display from a single cell is already described explicitly in the literature. A118108 and MathWorld give closed forms for every row (Weisstein 2006), and A.J. Macfarlane (2016, Fig. 8) gives the full two-variable generating function G54(t,x) of the display. The middle column 1,1,0,0 (period 4) follows at once from those rows. A077854 also records (Keller 2021) that the middle column, read in base 2, has g.f. 1/((1-x)(1-2x)(1+x^2)), the base-2 analogue. Barker's base-10 g.f. is then a direct rewrite. The Lean proof (induction giving the explicit pattern, then periodic digits) is genuine but reproves a known, essentially immediate fact.

mo-480222.reason: The formal statement models O_n as any nonzero unital C*-algebra generated by n isometries with sum s_i s_i* = 1, which is legitimate by Cuntz uniqueness. It asserts that positive matrices a, b over A satisfy a <~ b iff a = 0 or b != 0, i.e. W(O_n) = {0, infinity}. The MathOverflow question was answered in a comment by Jamie Gabe right after it was posed: a simple C*-algebra is purely infinite iff Cu(A) = {0, infinity}, which then agrees with W(A), so Cu(O_n) = W(O_n) = {0, infinity}. He calls this 'an easy exercise'. The statement file itself cites this comment as the answer. The Lean proof is a long and genuine formalization of the standard pure-infiniteness argument, but the question was a request for a known fact and was already answered at the source.

Green51.green_51.one_half.reason: The upstream statement green_51.one_half says: for each k > 0 there is c such that, for large n, every A in F_2^n of density > 1/2 - k/sqrt(n) has a coset of dimension >= n - c in A+A. The PR file says it is an 'Independent Lean 4 formalization of the proof by Jensen Kohlmeyer and Liam Kruer', and the PR body states that it adapts Faldor's formalization. The proof is genuine, but the result is not new.

The terms of A002486 (convergent denominators of pi) also give infinitely many members. The result was already known.
